title: MuellerPT: Decomposition Driven Pre-training for Dense Learning in Mueller Polarimetry
reviewer_1_strengths: The core idea of using Lu-Chipman decomposition as a physics-grounded pretext task is well-motivated and elegant. Unlike generic self-supervised objectives (contrastive loss, masked autoencoders), this approach grounds representation learning directly in the optical physics of Mueller polarimetry. The dual-stream architecture separating polarimetric content (fθ) from intensity (mψ) seems reasonable and allows for situations where downstream datasets lacking the un-normalized m(0,0) channel. The label-efficiency gains are compelling. The 20% absolute DICE improvement at 5% training data and the 8% accuracy gain at 1% for classification are substantial, and the benefit to the minority class (white matter) is particularly encouraging for clinical applicability, where rare tissue classes are often the most diagnostically important.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The comparison baseline is narrow. The paper only compares MuellerPT against HRNet-Scratch (random initialization). There is no comparison against: (1) ImageNet pre-trained initialization, (2) generic SSL methods (e. g. , SimCLR, MAE, DINO) applied to Mueller data, or (3) using the Lu-Chipman maps directly as input features without pre-training. This makes it difficult to attribute the gains specifically to the physics-grounded pretext task versus simply the benefit of any form of pre-training. A frozen encoder baseline would also help disentangle the benefit of pre-training from fine-tuning dynamics. The MAP-Org dataset (41 images) is quite small for a pre-training corpus, and it is composed exclusively of animal food tissue (lamb, chicken, steak, bacon). The paper does not analyze how dataset size or tissue diversity affect downstream performance. An ablation on pre-training data scale, or a comparison pre-training on a subset of MAP-Org vs. the full set, would substantially strengthen the empirical claims. Lack of ablation experiments make design choices and their relative contribution toward improvement in performance difficult to interpret. For example, two-stream architecture vs single-stream architecture is proposed but the relative contribution of single stream is not ablated. The authors acknowledge in the introduction that Lu-Chipman decompositions are sensitive to measurement noise and depolarization behaviour, yet no sensitivity analysis is conducted to examine how decomposition quality affects pre-training. Inclusion of such results would strengthen the quality of the paper and ensure that the results are generalization and due to contribution of Lu-Chipman decomposition.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.An interesting and relatively under-researched problem setting. This paper explores Mueller matrix polarization measurements, an area far less saturated than mainstream medical imaging. The proposed approach—designing a pre-trained target based on polarization physics principles, rather than simply importing a generic SSL target—is well-motivated and potentially valuable to the field. Using Lu-Chipman decomposition as the structured target is particularly appealing because it is physically meaningful and requires minimal manual annotation. 2.A physics-based pre-training task is a significant contribution. The mapping obtained from the predicted decomposition is a plausible pre-training signal: it is task-relevant, associated with known optical structures, and more consistent with downstream domains than generic contrast or reconstruction targets. This paper strongly demonstrates that this supervised approach can encourage the generation of representations that reflect tissue microstructure rather than merely surface image statistics. 3.This paper contributes a new dataset resource. The MAP-Org dataset itself appears to be a valuable contribution. Despite its relatively small absolute size, collecting 41 multispectral Mueller matrix images covering various animal tissues for pre-training is no easy feat in this field, and the public availability of this dataset enhances the potential impact of this work. 4.Evaluation on two downstream tasks is a wise design choice. This paper does not validate on only one downstream benchmark. It tests the pre-trained representations on two tasks: dense segmentation (PoLambRimetry) and image-level classification (ColoPola), making the conclusions of transfer learning more convincing than single-task evaluations. 5.The focus on few-shot training is appropriate. Performance improvements are primarily concentrated in low-label regions, consistent with the research motivation of this paper. In the segmentation task, significant performance improvements are achieved compared to the initial baseline at 1% and 5% label availability; in the classification task, improvements at 1% and 5% label availability are also practically meaningful. This is precisely the area where domain-specific pre-training methods are most effective. 6.This paper includes cross-sample segmentation evaluation. For the PoLambRimetry, sample-level splitting using nested cross-validation is appropriate and helps reduce data leakage. This is an advantage, especially in small biomedical datasets where leakage between slices or samples is a common problem. 7.This paper includes domain offset analysis. Qualitative experiments on isolated human esophageal tissue, particularly with a simplified Mueller matrix configuration, are an interesting attempt to show that the learned representations can generalize beyond the precise pre-training domain, even tolerating hardware simplifications. While this is not a complete quantitative validation, it is a useful and thoughtful addition.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The empirical comparison scope is too narrow. The primary comparison is with the same HRNet architecture trained entirely from scratch. This is a fair and important baseline, but insufficient to prove the correctness of the proposed pre-training task. The paper demonstrates the value of Lu-Chipman prediction as a pre-training task, but does not compare it with other stronger pre-training schemes. 2.The pre-training dataset is small, and the paper may have exaggerated its scalability. MAP-Org contains 41 multispectral Mueller matrix images from fresh animal tissues. This is useful in this subdomain, but the paper also describes the method as a way to “scale up pre-training.” Considering the size of the real-world dataset, this statement seems somewhat idealistic. 3.Downstream results are positive, but the advantage gradually disappears as the label ratio increases. The results show that the method is mainly effective with few samples, and when the label ratio reaches 25%, 50%, and 100%, the difference between MuellerPT and the Scratch baseline in both segmentation and classification becomes very small. This contribution is best viewed as an improvement in low-label efficiency rather than a general performance improvement. 4.Ablation experiments need enhancement. This method combines several elements: Lu-Chipman prediction, a two-stream architecture with separated normalized Mueller data and m(0,0) channels, hardware-heuristic dropout, and Mueller-specific data augmentation. Since only the overall method is compared to the initial training, it is unclear which components are most important. This is a major technical shortcoming of this paper. 5.Limited comparison with task-specific non-pre-trained alternatives. This paper proposes a pre-trained task partly for the interpretability of Lu-Chipman parameters, but does not compare it with simpler alternatives. Therefore, it is impossible to determine whether the performance improvement stems from pre-training itself or simply from injecting decomposition-derived prior information in some way.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper presents a physics-guided pretraining approach that uses Lu–Chipman decomposition maps as pretraining targets. This is a strong idea because these maps encode meaningful polarimetric tissue properties while avoiding the need for manual labels. Since Lu–Chipman decomposition provides a standard physical interpretation of Mueller matrices into diattenuation, retardance, and depolarization-related components, the pretext task is aligned with the imaging physics rather than relying on a generic computer vision task. The paper also addresses the important practical problem of label efficiency, as dense annotations in biomedical polarimetry are scarce, and the reported few shot experiments directly target this limitation. The strongest gains are observed in low-label settings, especially for white matter segmentation with 5% training data and colorectal classification accuracy with 1% and 5% training data. The evaluation uses relevant public biomedical polarimetry datasets, including PoLambRimetry for segmentation and ColoPola for colorectal cancer classification. The two-stream design is also reasonable, as separating the intensity like m(0,0) channel from the normalized polarimetric stream is physically motivated and consistent with earlier Mueller learning work such as MuellerNet. The reduced Mueller experiment is interesting and clinically relevant because reduced polarimetric systems can be faster and simpler.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper has several limitations that should be addressed. The main comparison is too limited because MuellerPT is evaluated mainly against the same HRNet architecture trained from scratch. While this isolates the benefit of pre-training over random initialization, it does not show whether Lu–Chipman prediction is better than other plausible pretraining strategies. Stronger baselines should include at least one generic self-supervised learning method, such as contrastive learning or masked autoencoding, and preferably an ImageNet- or medical-pretrained baseline adapted to the same input structure. The ablation studies are also insufficient, as the paper does not clearly quantify the contribution of each design component, including the Lu–Chipman pretext target, Mueller element dropout, the two-stream m(0,0)/polarimetric design, physical realizability filtering, Mueller-specific rotations, and MAP-Org pre-training scale. Without these ablations, it is difficult to determine whether the gains come from the proposed physics-guided target or from other training details. The MAP-Org dataset is described as large, but only 41 multispectral Mueller matrix images are reported, so the manuscript should provide the effective number of samples or patches, tissue-level splits, wavelengths, spatial resolution, number of specimens per organ type, and pretraining/validation split. The classification split may also risk data leakage because random 60/20/20 splits are used for ColoPola, and the manuscript should clarify whether multiple slices could come from the same patient or tissue block. The qualitative human esophagus experiment is promising, but it is not enough to support strong robustness claims because it appears to rely on one ex vivo human sample and qualitative assessment only. The paper should soften claims about robustness to tissue or domain shift unless quantitative evaluation across more human samples and acquisition settings is added. Statistical testing is also missing, as the paper reports mean ± standard deviation over runs but does not provide confidence intervals, paired tests, or effect-size analysis, which is important because some improvements at 25–100% labels are small. Finally, the implementation details are incomplete, and the manuscript should include the loss function, optimizer, learning rates, batch size, patch size, training epochs, augmentation probabilities, dropout configurations, and exact downstream heads to support reproducibility.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We would like to thank the reviewers and meta reviewer for their time and thoughtful feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers had a generally positive view on MuellerPT. We address the concerns raised and minor adjustments will be made to the camera-ready submission. As the reviews have several similar comments, we present the response to the general concerns mentioned by the meta-reviewer first and then address the remaining individual reviewer comments. Baselines (R1, R2, R3, R4, MR): Our study was designed as a first evaluation. The architecture, splits and training schedules are fixed with only the weight initialisation changing. This isolates whether decomposition driven pretraining provides useful representations under scarce labels. Comparisons to generic SSL methods is an interesting suggestion for future work and will allow an empirical evaluation of the Lu-Chipman pretext task in comparison to generic SSL methods. Ablation study (R1, R2, R3, MR): This study evaluates the complete MuellerPT pipeline and does not provide experiments disentangling the contribution of the two-stream architecture, Mueller specific augmentations, element dropout, and Lu-Chipman target. The two stream design was found to lead to more physically plausible Lu-Chipman reconstructions, the Mueller augmentations increased dataset diversity, leading to improved generalizability and the element dropout was used to encourage learning of an ill-formed Lu-Chipman process (as opposed to simply using the numerical derivation) as seen in Figure 4.A comprehensive quantitative ablation study is an important area for future work to pinpoint which design choices lead to the best performance, although we believe this experiment would not fundamentally change the argument of our study which supports the use of Lu-Chipman as a pretraining task for biomedical Mueller polarimetry. Reproducibility (R1, R3, MR): The full code repository and MAP-Org dataset will be released at publication and included in the camera-ready submission to allow for re-implementation. Data leakage (R3, MR): The train/val/test split employed for the ColoPola dataset is similar to the split used by the original author. The ColoPola paper has the limitation that it does not provide information on whether the slices come from different patients or tissue blocks. This is therefore beyond our control, and we agree that caution should be taken when evaluating the benefits of MuellerPT on ColoPola. We nonetheless believe it to be a valuable source of preliminary evidence of image level transfer. Size of MAP-ORG (R1, R2, R3, R4): Each acquisition contains six wavelengths and dense 4x4 Mueller matrices over high resolution fields of view. However, we agree that MAP-Org is modest in terms of specimen level count and our intention is that MAP-Org is useful as a pretraining resource for biomedical Mueller polarimetry, where publicly available Mueller matrix datasets are limited. Human oesophagus experiment (R3, R4): We agree that the human oesophagus experiment should not be interpreted as quantitative evidence of robust clinical generalisation due to its limited size. The sample was chosen as a representative example human case, and although results were consistent across multiple samples, further quantitative analysis is needed. Sensitivity analysis for Lu-Chipman decomposition quality (R1): In our pipeline Lu-Chipman targets are computed after normalization and validity checks. Invalid or numerically unstable pixels are excluded to prevent any noise bias. A sensitivity analysis on how Lu-Chipman quality impacts training is an interesting extension although given the focus of this study on physically valid pixels, this would not fundamentally change the argument of our study. Methodology novelty (R4): The novelty is not the architectural or optimization framework but instead the formulation of a Mueller polarimetry specific dense pretext task based on Lu-Chipman decomposition.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This manuscript introduces a physics guided pre-training approach for segmentation and classification tasks in Mueller Polarimetry, based on a newly acquired dataset. Reviewers thought that this work represents a clear, well-motivated and elegant technical contribution in an under-researched area, combined with a new dataset resource. Their main concern was narrow experimental comparisons, in particular, not accounting for any plausible alternative pre-training strategies. Moreover, given that the proposed method consists of multiple components, ablations would help identify those that are most relevant. Since no new experimental results are allowed in the rebuttal, I do not expect it would provide substantial new information for making a decision. As it stands, reviewers are on the positive side overall. In the final version, authors will need to address the potential data leakage in their classification results (suspected by reviewer 3) and issues of reproducibility, which were another major concern among reviewers.

title: Mutually Promoted Medical Image Segmentation and Classification via Prompt-Driven Interaction
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper provides a novel integrated SAM-classification framework (C2FM, GFE, SACS modules) with well structured methodology and ablation. It demonstrates strong validation with benchmark methods on 6 datasets, and shows competitive performance results. Overall, there is clinical potential as the method potentially improves interpretability.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limitations include the reliance on manual box prompts, rather than a fully automated and scalable clinical workflow. There is incomplete evaluation (eg metrics limited to DSC/IOU), and the classification results are somewhat weak on key datasets (such as AbdomenCT1K). SACS is presented as one of the major contributions but not isolated in the ablation (bundled within TG). There are also some missing elements for reproducibility, e. g. the LLM is never identified or cited.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Innovative mutually reinforcing framework: By explicitly modeling the bidirectional interaction between segmentation and hierarchical classification, the proposed BiMI framework effectively addresses the issue of semantic inconsistency and improves the anatomical plausibility of medical image segmentation. 2.Technical contributions: The Coarse-to-Fine Matrix (C2FM) provides a soft regularization mechanism to alleviate data scarcity in fine-grained classification. The Global-to-Local Feature Enhancement (GFE) module successfully aligns global and local features. In addition, the Structure-Aware Candidate Selection (SACS) module cleverly leverages text-guided semantic priors to resolve the inherent multi-mask ambiguity of SAM. 3.Comprehensive experimental validation: The authors conduct extensive experiments on six diverse public datasets covering multiple imaging modalities (CT, MRI, dermoscopy, and endoscopy) and targets (organs and lesions). The results demonstrate that BiMI outperforms both U-Net-based baselines and recent SAM-based baselines on both segmentation and classification tasks.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Dependence on manual bounding-box prompts: The current framework relies on manually provided bounding-box prompts for localization, which limits its feasibility in fully automatic clinical applications. Although the authors mention adaptive bounding-box refinement as a direction for future work, they should more carefully discuss the practical clinical relevance of manual prompting compared with fully automatic segmentation pipelines, and possibly consider a user study to justify this design choice. 2.Computational overhead and complexity: Integrating a frozen large language model (LLM), a text encoder (CLIP), and the SAM architecture introduces substantial computational complexity. The paper lacks a detailed analysis of inference time, memory consumption, and overall computational cost in comparison with simpler baseline models such as nnU-Net or standard SAM. 3.Lack of discussion of failure cases: Although the quantitative results are strong, the paper would benefit from a more in-depth qualitative analysis of failure cases.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This method achieves a unified framework for multi-task collaborative optimization and cross-modal knowledge fusion through an innovative bidirectional mutually reinforcing architecture of segmentation and classification, a hierarchical semantic constraint C2FM module, and text-guided anatomical rationality verification. 2.The proposed feature alignment mechanism retains global discriminative power, avoiding over-alignment. Cross-attention enables dynamic information interaction. 3.The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The manuscript does not follow the MICCAI26 format. 2.The major limitation of this methos is the requirement of manual provision of bounding boxes to locate the target region. The paper acknowledges this in the Conclusion but does not provide a solution. 3.Insufficient validation of the necessity of the two-stage training strategy. Why freeze C2FM training for 50 epochs before joint training in the second stage? Has end-to-end training been attempted? What is the performance difference? 4.The compared SAM-based methods (MedSAM, SAM-Med2D, etc.) are all from 2023-2024.Lack of comparison with stronger baselines like SAM2 and MedSAM2.5.Insufficient interpretability of the SACS module. Definitions of descriptors (compactness, solidity, connectivity, gradient entropy) are not given in the text. 6.As can be seen from Table 3, all performance aspects decreased after adding GFE. So what is the point of adding this module?
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and reviewers for their time and constructive feedback. We are encouraged by their acknowledgement of the novelty and the superior results of our work. Below we do our best to resolve the key concerns raised by them. 1.Format. We apologize for the confusing running header. We used the official MICCAI 2026 template without modifying margins, font, spacing, or page limit. We will correct the missing short title. 2.GFE. The performance drop in Table 3 occurs only for GFE without FA (i.e., unaligned global feature injection), not the complete design. This verifies our hypothesis in Sec. 2.2: direct global-local fusion may cause semantic misalignment. SA+TG+C2FM gives 78.8/87.3 IoU/DSC; unaligned GFE drops to 73.9/85.3; adding FA gives the best 79.1/87.7.These results do prove the effectiveness of our method. 3.Training. C2FM is not a trainable branch. It serves as a coarse-to-fine prior for the classifier. According to our experience, direct end-to-end coupling of C2FM and other modules would result in unstable training behavior. We believe this is because early inaccurate class predictions can mislead mask selection, while early coarse predictions also introduce noisy priors for fine classification. Thus, we first stabilize the segmentation-related components and classifier, and then integrate them via C2FM, GFE/FA, and SACS. 4.SAM2/MedSAM2.Our comparison focuses on representative U-Net-based and medical SAM-based baselines under the same 2D slice-wise box-prompt protocol. SAM2/MedSAM2 are mainly designed for image-video or 3D propagation settings; while their native protocol defines different tasks, forcing single-slice inference would not reflect their intended design. As for BiMI, its contribution is the segmentation-classification interaction mechanism, which is orthogonal to the SAM backbone. 5.SACS/TG. Sorry for the unclear notation. In Table 3, TG is actually TG with SACS (or TG/SACS) rather than an independent text-only module: it denotes the text-guided candidate-selection path implemented by SACS. Text embeddings are mapped to structural weights. SACS combines them with mask descriptors and SAM’s IoU prediction to rank candidates and select the final mask. Because text is not injected into the decoder, TG without SACS is undefined in our architecture. Our early trial shows that direct text-feature concatenation did not work in practice, which motivates SACS. In Table 3, the TG on/off comparison corresponds to the SACS-path on/off ablation, improving IoU/DSC from 78.0/86.1 to 78.5/86.9.We will rename TG as TG/SACS. 6.Cost, LLM, and ethics. Our BiMI’s online overhead mainly comes from the classifier, GFE/FA, and SACS candidate-mask scoring. The language step is offline: GPT-4 generates coarse/fine label-pair descriptions once, and CLIP encodes them into a precomputed embedding bank. At inference, BiMI only retrieves the embedding for the predicted label pair and applies descriptor-based ranking to SAM candidates, with no per-image LLM call. Apart from SAM and the classifier, the language-guided SACS overhead is limited to embedding lookup, mask-descriptor computation, and score fusion. The LLM receives no patient images, masks, metadata, or clinical notes, and is not used for diagnosis or treatment decisions. Therefore, its use does not incur patient-data privacy or LLM-driven clinical-decision risks. 7.Prompting and evaluation. We acknowledge that BiMI is not fully automatic. We use the same box-prompt interface as SAM-style baselines, adding no extra localization burden. DSC/IoU were used because they are consistently reported across the six datasets for fair comparison. AbdomenCT1K is difficult for all classifiers due to similar slice-level CT appearances, but BiMI remains best under the same protocol.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Scores are 4/4/2, with two reviewers recommending weak accept and one PhD-student reviewer recommending reject “independent of rebuttal” on the basis of format non-compliance, the GFE-hurts-performance ablation, missing modern baselines, and insufficient training-strategy validation. The paper is borderline-leaning-positive, but several of R3’s concerns — particularly the GFE ablation contradiction and the format compliance — are concrete enough that a credible rebuttal is required to retain the weak accepts. The paper is invited for rebuttal; authors should prioritize (a) a direct, principled explanation of the GFE ablation result that shows performance decreasing when GFE is added, (b) at least one comparison against SAM 2 / MedSAM 2 or a clear justification for omitting them, (c) a properly isolated SACS ablation and an end-to-end vs. two-stage training comparison, (d) computational-cost analysis and identification of the LLM used in SACS, and (e) clarification of the ethics concern flagged by R1. | Reviewers agreed that the bidirectional segmentation-classification framework is novel and well-motivated, the three modules (C2FM, GFE, SACS) are clean, the multi-modality evaluation across six datasets is comprehensive, and the clinical potential for interpretability is meaningful. They raised several concerns: (1) reliance on manual bounding-box prompts limits clinical deployment in fully automatic workflows; (2) computational overhead from integrating LLM + CLIP + SAM is not analyzed; (3) recent stronger SAM-family baselines (SAM2, MedSAM2) are missing; (4) the two-stage training strategy is not validated against end-to-end coupling; (5) SACS is bundled with TG in ablation, making its individual contribution unclear; (6) GFE alone (without FA) degrades performance, raising intrinsic-reliability concerns; (7) manuscript format issues (running header, references vs. bibliography); (8) the LLM is not explicitly identified or cited; and (9) failure case analysis is missing.After rebuttal, the authors clarified that GFE’s degradation occurs only without the FA alignment component (the full design achieves the best 79.1/87.7 IoU/DSC), justified the two-stage training based on instability of direct C2FM end-to-end coupling, argued SAM2/MedSAM2 target different protocols (video/3D propagation) orthogonal to BiMI’s contribution, renamed TG to TG/SACS to clarify the ablation, explained that the LLM/CLIP pipeline is offline (no per-image LLM call, no patient data exposure), and confirmed the box-prompt protocol matches SAM baselines. However, the most critical reviewer maintained that the manual-prompt limitation remains, the two-stage training justification is empirical without quantitative ablation, the SAM2/MedSAM2 absence remains a real comparison gap, and GFE’s dependence on FA raises intrinsic-reliability concerns. Final scores are split (Accept, Accept, Reject). Overall, the AC believes that the merits outweigh the drawbacks and recommend accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After rebuttal the reviews stand at two leaning accept and one reject. The rebuttal does clarify the format and SACS/TG notation issues and gives a self-consistent account of the GFE+FA design, and the two positive reviewers are satisfied. However, the concerns that bear on the paper’s contribution remain. The method is one of many incremental SAM box-prompt adaptations, and the ablation shows the full design improves only marginally over SA+TG+C2FM, with GFE actually degrading performance unless paired with FA — which weakens the case for it as a standalone contribution. Given the limited novelty and marginal gains relative to existing SAM-prompt methods, I lean toward rejection despite the rebuttal’s clarifications, as a borderline case. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Two reviewers recommended acceptance after rebuttal, recognizing the innovative framework and comprehensive validation. The authors’ rebuttal partially addressed R3’s concerns. Although some minor concerns such as relying on manual box prompts and comparison with SAM2 remain, I believe they don’t overweigh the contribution.

title: Non-intrusive Body Composition Assessment from Full-Body mmWave Scans
reviewer_1_strengths: The primary strength of this paper is the introduction of a novel imaging-based approach for body composition assessment using mmWave data. This represents an innovative alternative to traditional modalities such as CT and MRI, offering a solution that is potentially lower-cost, faster, and non-invasive, while still aiming to capture clinically relevant metrics such as visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and body fat percentage (BFP). This makes the approach promising for large-scale, opportunistic screening of metabolic diseases. Another key strength is the strategy used to address the lack of paired mmWave and CT/MRI datasets. The authors leverage prior information from publicly available full-body CT and MRI datasets to guide the learning process. The paper also tackles the challenge of differing acquisition conditions (e. g. , subject positioning differences between mmWave and CT/MRI). From a methodological perspective, the use of vision transformer–based models for estimating VAT and BFP from mmWave and prior information derived from MRI/CT datasets is a relevant choice. Applying such architectures to this type of data and task demonstrates originality and extends the application of transformer-based models to a less explored imaging domain. The work could enable non-invasive and accessible body composition assessment, facilitate early detection and monitoring of metabolic conditions in broader populations.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The authors do not provide validation against gold-standard measurements such as paired CT or MRI scans. Instead, the evaluation relies on indirect comparisons, which limits confidence in the accuracy of the estimated VAT and BFP. The test cohort appears to be small, which may raise concerns about the generalisability of the results.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper proves the potential of using mmWave scanners for BCA measurement.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The network design appears to lack sufficient novelty, as the architecture relies on a standard Point Transformer backbone with multiple classification heads. 2.The paper lacks a comparison with existing methodologies. It is highly recommended to identify and include other relevant BCA methods to provide a clearer context for evaluating the proposed approach. 3.Table 1 does not present the main results of the proposed method. 4.The paper suffers from a lack of comprehensive experimental analysis. a) The reason why mmWave point clouds can estimate VAT and BFP is not well justified, which raises concerns about the generalization capability of the proposed method—i.e., whether the method performs well on unseen subjects (not included in training). b) The quality of the collected mmWave points is essential for subsequent measurements, but the authors did not analyze its impact. c) The material of clothing should affect the mmWave points, yet no relevant experiments were conducted to evaluate this effect. d) It is important to report the distribution of body shape, age, gender, and other relevant information, as the diversity of human subjects is crucial for demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. e) Other conditions—such as the motion of the human subject, the distance between the front and back mmWave scanners, and long-term measurements of the same subject—are also important impact factors, but they are not mentioned.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The authors solve the data problem by turning MRI/CT scans into 3D point clouds. Using the SMPL model to fix the pose difference between lying down and standing. The methodology demonstrates that Multi-Task Learning (MTL) provides significant advantages in data-constrained environments. By predicting anatomical measures (such as height and waist circumference) alongside internal fat volumes and showing improved performance in correlation between VAT and BF when compared to single-task baselines. The paper includes Masked Sample Loss and dynamic weighted objective as an optimization approach to balance task-specific gradients and ensuring model convergence across targets.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The authors excluded 41 scans due to extreme body fat values. Given that individuals with high visceral fat are the primary target population for metabolic screening, does this exclusion limit the clinical utility of the system? It would be beneficial to discuss why these anatomical extremes are challenging. In Table 1, the reported SAT and VAT MAE values appear high relative to measurements of typical SAT VAT range[1]. Could the authors provide more context or intuition as to why this is? Lastly, the authors compare a baseline trained only on CT/MRI against the full MTL pipeline. However, the intermediate step of MRI/CT + SMPL or MRI/CT+mmWave is missing. [1] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3636065/
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful comments. Reviewers highlighted the novelty of the mmWave imaging modality for body composition assessment (BCA) (R1,R2,R3,M2), the contribution of the multi-modal, multi-source synthetic-to-real pipeline (R1,R3,M2), and the strong motivation of providing nonintrusive, accessible imaging for personalized medicine (R1,R2,M2) and opportunistic screening of metabolic diseases (R1). Novelty (R2): While we agree that the model architecture uses established point cloud encoders, we would argue for the novelty of leveraging mmWave scans for BCA, with the goal of enabling non-intrusive, personalized medicine. This modality has not previously been considered for this task, and as noted by M2, the main contribution lies in the synthetic-to-real pipeline which enables model training. Comprehensive, longitudinal, gold-standard evaluation (R1,R2.d,e, M2): We share the reviewers’ desire for comprehensive, longitudinal data collection with gold standard ground truth for BCA. Nevertheless, we believe our results, which explore mmWave scans as a medical imaging modality for the first time, prove the potential of this modality, motivating the time and cost investment necessary for large-scale, long-term data collection. We will update our discussion to point toward this future work. Acquisition variability (R2.b,c,e): We agree that scan variability, e.g. demographics, clothing, and pose, are important for validation. In our real data collection, each participant underwent three consecutive scans to account for pose and noise variability, with predictions averaged across measurements. Participants were clothed in streetwear to emulate casual acquisitions and instructed to stand on fixed floor markers in a standard A-pose. Participants ranged from 21 to 31 years old, from 51 to 108 kg, and consisted of 8 men, 6 women. We will clarify these points in the experimental description. Baselines (R2.a): While related work estimates BCA based on full-body meshes, this is the first work exploring mmWave scans as a medical imaging modality. As M2 notes, the primary contribution lies in the synthetic-to-real pipeline: CT/MRI-derived point clouds, SMPL-based pose bridging, and masked multi-task learning. We will clarify that our evaluation of these components demonstrates that they make BCA from mmWave scans possible. Exclusion of outliers (R3): We agree that BCA methods should be performative across a range of body shapes, and the reviewer’s comment points toward a potential limitation of the current pipeline. At the low end (<5% BFP), even “minimally decomposed” samples can carry anatomical artifacts corrupting TotalSegmentator-derived BCA values. At the high end, (>70% BFP), field-of-view truncation made both labels and surfaces impossible to obtain. We will acknowledge these limitations in the CR. Intermediate ablations (R3): We share the reviewer’s desire to improve our data pipeline by exhaustively isolating the contribution of each component, e.g. by ablating SMPL-based or real data. Nevertheless, we believe our results demonstrate the feasibility of BCA estimation from mmWave scans, an imaging modality never before considered in this context, and the contribution of the multi-headed training pipeline to enable synthetic-to-real training. Minor comments (R3): We will provide context for SAT and VAT MAE values, which are affected by annotator variability regarding the boundaries of the abdomen.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This submission presents a novel and technically coherent feasibility study on body composition assessment from full-body mmWave scans, addressing an important clinical-monitoring problem through a non-intrusive and privacy-preserving sensing modality. The strengths of the paper are the originality of the application setting and the integrated methodological design used to address the lack of paired mmWave and gold-standard imaging data. In particular, the manuscript combines synthetic mmWave-like point cloud generation from CT/MRI, SMPL-based handling of posture mismatch, and partial-label multi-task learning in a way that is well aligned with the stated problem. The paper also provides initial real-data evidence, including improved pilot-cohort correlations over a simpler single-head baseline, which supports the core feasibility claim. The decisive concerns relate to the strength and scope of the validation. After checking the manuscript, it is clear that the real body-composition evaluation is based on a small pilot cohort and uses bioimpedance rather than paired CT/MRI as reference, which limits the strength of clinical conclusions. In addition, applicability to extreme body-fat cases and robustness across acquisition conditions are not fully characterized. At the same time, some reviewer criticisms are only partially supported. In particular, the concern that the main results are missing from the paper appears to stem from a misunderstanding, since the relevant real-cohort BCA results are presented in Fig. 3, with an explicit explanation for using correlation rather than direct MAE. Likewise, the objection that the work lacks novelty is overstated if judged only at the encoder level, because the main contribution lies in the integrated synthetic-to-real training and domain-bridging pipeline.

title: Oneclass4ASD: Autism Spectrum Disorder Screening via One-class Classifier
reviewer_1_strengths: While there is no new core methodology introduced as such, this represents a good, novel pipeline consisting of existing components, solving a useful interesting problem in a straightforward manner.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the broader nature of the pipeline as a whole is mostly clear, the explanations provided can be a bit hand-wavy or lacking in detail at times, making the work harder to follow or be able to replicate the work fully (which is particularly important since no code is provided alongside the paper). Additionally, while they provide ablation studies showing the impact of some components compared to benchmarks, they do not provide much personal insight as to why one approach works and the other does not; they simply use these as evidence that “they happened to make good choices” somehow.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Oneclass approach may reduce reliance on difficult to measure cases, and shows better performance than baseline.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: THere are no major weaknesses to this paper.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The visualizations, together with the proposed framework, provide some evidence that the method is feasible and can effectively capture discriminative gaze-related patterns for ASD screening under the one-class setting.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Concern 1: Potential inconsistency in the two-stage design. The proposed two-stage framework raises questions regarding the actual interaction between its components. While the first stage is designed to predict fixation maps for healthy individuals, it is not clearly explained how these predictions are utilized in the second stage. In particular, the selection strategy for a fixed number of fixation points (e.g., 12) is not specified, and its connection to the predicted fixation maps remains unclear. Moreover, the extracted “1024-dimensional visual features” appear to be derived directly from the backbone network applied to the original images, rather than from the predicted fixation maps. This suggests that the first-stage model may not play a significant role during inference. Therefore, it would be helpful for the authors to clarify the dependency between the two stages and justify the necessity of this design. Concern 2: Practical limitations in testing flexibility. The proposed method appears to rely on aggregating features over a relatively large set of observed images (e.g., hundreds of stimuli) for each subject to compute uncertainty-aware weights. This raises questions about its practicality in real-world or clinical scenarios, where collecting such extensive observations for each new subject may not always be feasible. It would be helpful for the authors to clarify whether the method can generalize to settings with fewer observations or more flexible testing conditions. Concern 3: While the use of Deep SVDD enables modeling deviations from healthy patterns, it may be inherently limited in distinguishing the underlying causes of such deviations. For instance, individuals with other neurodevelopmental conditions (e.g., ADHD or intellectual disabilities) may also exhibit atypical gaze patterns. It is therefore unclear how the model would differentiate ASD-specific patterns from other forms of deviation, and whether this could lead to potential misclassification. Further discussion or empirical evaluation on this aspect would strengthen the work. Concern 4: Questionable extent of data efficiency gains. The paper emphasizes alleviating the difficulty of collecting ASD data by adopting a one-class learning paradigm. While this may reduce the need for ASD samples during training, it is less clear whether the overall data collection burden is substantially reduced. For example, the testing phase and the construction of subject-level representations still seem to require a considerable amount of eye-tracking data. It would be valuable for the authors to more carefully discuss the trade-offs and practical implications in terms of data efficiency compared to traditional binary classification approaches.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank Meta-Review (MR) and reviewers for valuable comments. MR, R4Q1, R5Q2: One-class assumption for multiple disorders. Thanks for your insight. The presence of other mental disorders during testing constitutes a typical open-set scenario, while our work primarily aims to provide autism clinicians with a screening tool for individuals visiting outpatient clinics with suspected symptoms. In open-set settings, traditional binary classification (ASD vs. TD) cannot reliably assess other disorders and only crudely separates individuals into ASD or TD. In contrast, our approach can determine whether an individual is neurotypical in this open-set scenario. Further analysis of other disorders would require additional approaches, such as cross-disorder classification. In future, we will test our approach to other disorders for more in-depth studies. MR, R4Q2: Two-stage design. Thanks. In our two-stage framework, the first stage trains VGG16 to extract gaze-related features using fixation maps from healthy individuals as supervision. These features guide the network to focus on fixation-relevant patterns but are not used to generate fixation maps. For each subject, the 12 fixation points are selected from the first 12 points in their recorded gaze sequence. The 1024-d features for the second stage are extracted from the backbone using the collected fixation coordinates on the input images, highlighting the necessity of the two-stage design. MR, R4Q3: Testing flexibility. Although our model requires participants to view hundreds of images, including 3s viewing and 1s break. Using our best model, 100 images takes only 6-7 minutes, while the image usage number can be flexibly adjusted. This free-viewing paradigm is noninvasive and easily implemented for patients. MR, R5Q1: Dataset size. We address potential overfitting by several complementary strategies across both model design and training. (1) We design a two-stage training framework which decouples the feature extraction and classification. The first stage uses an auxiliary task with fixation maps as supervision to guide feature extraction. This proxy loss instead of a direct classification loss reduces the risk of overfitting. (2) With 300 images per participant in Saliency4ASD, over 8,400 fixation maps provide rich features for the second stage, where a small mu and the soft-boundary objective further mitigate overfitting. (3) we adopt a 14-fold Leave-One-Out strategy to reduce bias, with comparable training and test performance further demonstrating the model’s stability and generalization. Nevertheless, we recognize that increasing the number of participants would further enhance model robustness. Since no other public datasets are available, we are collaborating with hospitals to collect more samples to improve the generalization of our approach in clinical settings. To R1 Q1-Q3: Clarification. Due to limit space, we cannot give a detailed explanation, but we promise to release the source code upon paper acceptance and carefully revise the paper to clarify our method. Q4-Q5: Softmax, Resnet-34 and cosine. Thanks. Due to page limits, we omitted detailed analysis. (1) Although the scores lie in (0, 1), they are not smooth enough, so Softmax is applied to improve performance. (2) VGG16 outperforms ResNet34 because the smaller fixation maps from ResNet-34 over-smooth the points. (3) Euclidean distance outperforms cosine, as fixation maps carry not only directional patterns but also magnitude and spatial density information. To R3 Q1-Q2: Clarification. Thanks. We will use neuraltypical for better intuition, and revise the paper carefully. To R4 Q4: Data collection burden To clarify, our work does not require ASD eye-tracking data for training, which addresses the challenge of the scarcity of ASD samples. While the testing phase requires constructing subject-level representations, each image only needs about 4s for viewing, which is the same as in binary-class method.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This submission reframes ASD screening from eye-tracking data as an anomaly detection problem, training only on healthy subjects to avoid reliance on scarce ASD data. Two reviewers (R1, R3) vote for accept and two reviewers (R4, R5) vote for weak reject. Significant concerns remain regarding methodological consistency, dataset scale, and practical applicability. The key points to address in the rebuttal are as follows: R5 highlights that the dataset is extremely small (14 ASD and 14 healthy subjects), raising serious concerns about overfitting, bias, and statistical reliability. R5 also questions whether the one-class assumption oversimplifies real-world clinical scenarios, where multiple disorders may exhibit similar gaze abnormalities. R4 notes that the relationship between stages in the framework is unclear and insufficiently justified. R4 raises concerns that the testing procedure may require extensive per-subject data aggregation, which could limit clinical usability. | Three reviewers recommend acceptance (one rising rating after rebuttal). The responses addressed the concerns about clinical usability and two-stage design. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The main merit of the paper is the reformulation of ASD screening as a one-class anomaly detection problem trained only on healthy subjects. This is a meaningful and clinically relevant perspective, since collecting reliable ASD eye-tracking data is difficult, and a sensitive screening tool can still provide value as part of a broader diagnostic workflow. The proposed framework is well motivated and demonstrates promising results despite the challenging low-data setting. Some concerns remain, particularly regarding the limited statistical reliability due to the small dataset size and the unclear applicability to broader neurodevelopmental conditions beyond ASD. Nevertheless, I think that the practical motivation, problem formulation, and encouraging empirical results outweigh these weaknesses. I therefore recommend acceptance. The remaining limitations should be clearly discussed in the final version. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper was initially invited for rebuttal following the primary review period, where reviewers raised several concerns regarding methodological consistency, dataset scale, and practical applicability. This paper got four reviews, of which three were accept in post-rebuttal. After carefully evaluating the authors’ rebuttal, the reviewers’ revised feedback, and re-examining the paper, I conclude that the authors have effectively addressed the key concerns raised, and the work now meets MICCAI’s publication standards

title: OrthoMorphNet: Alignment-Guided Hierarchical Morphological Synthesis of Post-orthodontic Dentition and Gingiva
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The manuscript is well organized and clearly written. 2.The paper addresses a real clinical problem in digital orthodontics by predicting gingival soft-tissue deformation after tooth movement, rather than focusing only on rigid tooth alignment. 3.This paper provides a comprehensive evolution of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.In Fig. 3, the visual improvements over the competing methods seem relatively limited, which makes the superiority reported in Table 2 less convincing and raises concerns about the consistency between the qualitative presentation and the numerical evaluation. 2.The approach converts intraoral scan data into volumetric representations and applies a transformer-based 3D encoder–decoder, which is technically reasonable, but this design is still relatively close to existing volumetric medical-image reconstruction pipelines. As a result, the innovation beyond integrating the two stages is not fully compelling. 3.The study relies on a public dataset, but it does not include internal or more challenging clinical cases, particularly patients with substantial gingival changes after orthodontic treatment. This limits the evidence for the model’s robustness and practical generalizability in more complex scenarios.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper introduces the first framework for jointly predicting post-treatment tooth alignment and the corresponding gingival morphology. Existing methods primarily focus on rigid tooth repositioning, whereas accurate gingival modeling is equally critical for realistic orthodontic simulation. In this regard, the paper pioneers a novel direction that has largely been overlooked in previous research.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper claims to propose a hierarchical framework for the joint synthesis of post-orthodontic dentition and gingiva. However, the tooth alignment and gingiva synthesis components appear largely independent. In other words, the tooth alignment module could be readily replaced by other state-of-the-art methods without affecting the overall pipeline. 2.The tooth alignment network lacks novelty. It encodes each tooth point cloud along with the set of tooth centers to regress translation and rotation, which is a commonly adopted strategy in existing methods (e.g., TANet). Essentially, the approach mainly replaces the encoder without introducing substantial innovation. In addition, the design of the collision loss is not well justified. The paper also does not provide comparisons with state-of-the-art tooth alignment methods, and based on the reported results, the proposed method does not achieve the best performance even among the selected baselines. 3.Accurate gingival morphology is indeed essential. Existing solutions include geometry-based approaches such as Laplacian deformation. The proposed method can be viewed as a learning-based approach; however, the authors do not clearly justify the necessity of adopting a learning-based paradigm, nor do they provide comparisons with established geometry-based methods.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: -The words, tables, and figures are pretty clear, readable, and well-organized in this work. -Author’s proposal and articulation of algorithmic innovation are clinically novel and detailed in this paper, and show restrained exposition of its clinical application potential. -It successfully expands orthodontic AI beyond just hard-tissue arrangement. -The authors present a highly ambitious end-to-end pipeline that effectively integrates complex 3D multimodal features of both teeth and gingiva.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: -There appear to be minor paragraph-formatting issues in the manuscript. For example, in the Introduction, the text formatting seems inconsistent after Ref. [17]. The authors are encouraged to carefully proofread the manuscript and correct these issues before publication. -A comparison with current state-of-the-art commercial software is currently missing. If feasible, including such a baseline would substantially strengthen the practical relevance of the study and help position the proposed method against existing clinical solutions. -The proposed network appears to rely primarily on visual supervision, without incorporating explicit physical boundary constraints. This raises concerns regarding clinical feasibility, as the method may produce non-physical interpenetration or unrealistic gaps between the generated gingival surface and the predicted tooth positions. -The low-resolution voxelization and subsequent reconstruction process may introduce substantial smoothing and stair-step artifacts, which can irreversibly remove high-frequency geometric details, particularly around the gingival margin. Such fine anatomical details are clinically important and should be better preserved. -Because the loss terms are fully decoupled and no backward consistency constraints are imposed, the overall framework effectively behaves as a unidirectional cascade. As a result, upstream errors in tooth arrangement may accumulate and propagate downstream, potentially amplifying inaccuracies in the final gingival prediction. -Given the extremely complex and heavy architecture (stacking multiple Transformers and 3D Convs), it is highly recommended to report the inference time and memory footprint to evaluate its clinical feasibility.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We appreciate reviewers for their constructive comments. [Novelty & Clinical Motivation – R1,R2,R3] We appreciate the recognition of the clinical relevance of jointly predicting post-orthodontic dentition and gingival morphology. Our contribution is to formulate an alignment-guided framework where predicted post-treatment teeth explicitly condition learnable gingiva synthesis, rather than simply applying a volumetric reconstruction network. Existing orthodontic AI mainly focuses on rigid tooth repositioning, while our work addresses coupled hard/soft-tissue prediction for realistic simulation, aligner fitting, and gingival-margin/interproximal assessment. We will revise the manuscript to distinguish this contribution from conventional volumetric pipelines. [Modularity & Alignment Comparison – R2] We appreciate the concern that the alignment module could be replaced by other methods. We view this modularity as intended, since our main contribution is not a unique alignment backbone, but using predicted post-treatment dentition as a learnable deformation condition for gingiva synthesis. To ensure reproducible orthodontic planning, we use a deterministic, physically regularized alignment stage with collision and adjacency constraints, and compare with representative deterministic methods, TAligNet and TANet. Our method achieves the best ADD and rotation error, while TANet is slightly better only in translation error. The translation gap is small, 0.114mm (0.868 vs. 0.754mm), whereas our rotation improvement is larger, 3.6°, which is more relevant to angular tooth alignment and gingival-margin/interproximal morphology. [Geometry-Based Gingiva Modeling – R2] We thank the reviewer for noting geometry-based gingiva modeling and tooth-movement-driven deformation methods. We agree these are important prior works and will discuss them explicitly. Our intention is not to claim gingiva adaptation has no precedent, but to formulate it as a learnable, data-driven conditional synthesis problem: the model learns the mapping from pre-treatment gingiva/teeth and estimated post-treatment tooth positions to post-treatment gingival morphology, rather than relying on manually specified handles, boundary rules, or deformation parameters. Our current comparison focuses on reproducible 3D volumetric baselines under the same public dataset/training setting. We will state that geometry-based methods and commercial software were not included, and pursue such comparisons when feasible. [Qualitative & Quantitative Consistency – R1] We appreciate the concern that visual improvements in Fig. 3 appear limited compared with Table 2.The gains over UNETR are modest in some metrics, but consistent across MAE, R2, IoU, Dice, SDE, HD, and NC. We will revise Fig. 3 by enlarging gingival-margin/interproximal regions and using clearer distance maps. We will clarify that the gains reflect consistent local surface-error reduction rather than visually dramatic global shape changes. [Generalization & Robustness – R1,R3] We agree that validation on internal datasets and challenging cases with substantial gingival changes would strengthen robustness evidence. Our experiments use a public paired pre/post-treatment dataset to ensure reproducibility and fair comparison. We will state this limitation, avoid overclaiming clinical deployment, and pursue multi-center validation. [Physical Constraints & Efficiency – R3] The alignment stage includes collision and adjacency regularization to reduce inter-tooth interpenetration and preserve arch continuity. We agree that the gingiva stage could be improved with explicit tooth-gingiva boundary constraints and backward consistency. DPSR indicator grids were chosen for noise robustness and topology preservation, but fine details may be smoothed. We additionally profiled inference on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU: 0.214s per case with 4.27GB peak allocated VRAM (4.88GB reserved), indicating practical efficiency for preoperative planning.
