title: PC-Seg: Progressive Cross-View Consistency for 3D OCT Segmentation from Sparse 2D Annotations
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a practically important problem: how to train a 3D OCT segmentation model under sparse 2D annotation conditions. Rather than directly relying on dense voxel-wise supervision, the method uses cross-view consistency to progressively lift limited 2D supervision into 3D training signals, which is a meaningful direction for annotation-efficient OCT analysis. 2.A notable strength is that the method uses a single 2D model to exploit information from both standard B-scans and orthogonal slices, instead of introducing multiple view-specific models. This design is conceptually neat and provides a feasible route from sparse 2D supervision to 3D modeling. 3.The method makes good use of unlabeled data. By leveraging consistency across views, it generates volumetric pseudo-labels and thereby increases the utility of unlabeled orthogonal slices, reducing dependence on costly 3D annotation. 4.The paper is also well aligned with practical clinical needs. Training a 3D model from only sparse 2D slice annotations is attractive in settings where voxel-level annotation is prohibitively expensive, and the reported results suggest that the proposed framework can support 3D analysis under highly limited supervision. 5.The experimental design is reasonably comprehensive. The paper evaluates the method on two public datasets, includes comparisons under different annotation ratios, and benchmarks against both fully supervised and semi-supervised methods. This makes the empirical evaluation relevant to the low-annotation setting that motivates the work. 6.The progressive multi-stage training strategy is another appealing aspect of the paper. The staged transition from 2D learning to 3D modeling appears to stabilize training and to reduce error amplification from early pseudo-labels, which is particularly important in sparse-supervision settings.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The overall idea is interesting, but the methodological novelty appears to be more in the integration of existing ideas than in a fundamentally new modeling framework. Cross-view consistency, pseudo-labeling, co-training, and curriculum learning have all been explored in medical image segmentation. The main contribution here lies in how these components are combined for sparse-annotation 3D OCT segmentation. 2.The rationale for the five-stage curriculum design is not sufficiently explained. The paper does not clearly justify why five stages were chosen, nor does it provide enough analysis of whether this design is necessary or optimal. Additional details on stage duration, switching criteria, and model selection during pseudo-label generation would improve both clarity and reproducibility. 3.Some implementation details remain unclear. For example, the paper could more clearly explain how orthogonal slices are aligned within the 3D volume, how pseudo-labels are transferred between the 2D and 3D models, how the feedback loop between the two models is implemented, and how the confidence thresholds are applied in practice. These omissions make the method harder to reproduce. 4.The motivation in the introduction for why existing multi-view methods developed for CT or MRI may not transfer well to OCT is currently not fully convincing. In particular, the discussion would benefit from a clearer explanation of anisotropy and why it changes the applicability of prior approaches. 5.The framework figure is informative but visually dense, which makes the overall pipeline somewhat difficult to follow at first reading. 6.The paper would benefit from additional analysis of confidence threshold selection for pseudo-label generation, since these thresholds are likely to influence the stability and final performance of the multi-stage training pipeline. 7.Some parts of the experimental presentation could be improved. For example, Table 2 does not report statistical significance indicators and does not explain missing entries clearly. In Table 3, the distinction between fully supervised and semi-supervised methods, as well as the annotation ratios used by each method, should be made more explicit to ensure fair and reproducible comparison. 8.Figure 2 mainly presents comparisons with relatively weaker segmentation results and does not include stronger or more representative baselines. Including comparisons against stronger-performing methods would make the visual evidence more convincing. 9.The full pipeline is relatively complex, involving multiple training stages, repeated pseudo-label generation, and alternating 2D/3D optimization. While this design may improve stability, it also increases implementation burden and hyperparameter sensitivity compared with simpler end-to-end approaches. 10.The conclusion section would be stronger if it more explicitly discussed current limitations and future directions, rather than largely restating the paper’s main findings.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The motivation to bridge the gap between 2D slice-wise annotations and 3D spatial context in OCT while alleviating the overhead of training 3D models from scratch is clear and practically valuable. 2.The writing is straightforward, and the pipeline logic is well-illustrated.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The core concern is the novelty of the method. According to my understanding, PC-seg is a general pipeline which is not only suitable for OCT, but also for other volumetric images, like CT, MRI. If you have searched deep enough in sparsely annotated semi-supervised segmentation/barely-supervised medical image segmentation, you will find the core idea of PC-seg is not original or novel. Especially for SGTC (AAAI 2025) [1] and DeSCO (CVPR 2023) [2], which also exploit orthogonal 2D sparse annotations to generate pseudo labels and then co-train 3D models (semi-supervised pipeline). But the authors didn’t include these up-to-date methods into their baseline for comparison. Since from the methodology perspective, PC-Seg is a general method, why do the authors only conduct experiments on OCT, not MRI or CT? To sum up, the authors should extend their proposed PC-Seg into different datasets from other modalities like CT, MRI and include more relevant baseline methods for comparison. Why not directly use well-pretrained model to generate pseudo-label but choose warm-up training? More up-to-date semi-supervised methods for 3D medical image segmentation should also be included. 2.The information in Fig.1 is so insufficient. When cross-referencing with the methodology section, it becomes apparent that many critical details are not visually represented, such as the predictions under four perturbations (weak, feature-level, and two strong) and the cross-teaching strategy. Consequently, the core innovation is obscured, instead of a clear highlight, the figure presents a cumbersome five-stage training strategy. 3.Lack of significance test: In highly sparse annotation settings (e.g., 6 or 30 labels), deep learning models are notoriously sensitive to the random sampling of labeled data. The paper exclusively reports single-run mean values in Tables 1, 2, and 3 without variance/standard deviation or statistical significance tests (e.g., t-test). The marginal improvements in some settings (e.g., 0.9135 to 0.9174 for 60 labels) are mathematically unconvincing without robust statistical validation. [1] SGTC: Semantic-Guided Triplet Co-training for Sparsely Annotated Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation [2] Orthogonal Annotation Benefits Barely-supervised Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper proposes a novel curriculum learning framework, named PC-Seg (Progressive Cross-view Segmentation) for volumetric 3D segmentation of optical coherence tomography (OCT) images. As opposed to existing semi-supervised learning methods that process data slice-by-slice, PC-Seg exploits the inherent 3D spatial context of OCT imaging data. Novel curriculum learning framework implemented in five stages lifts sparse 2D annotations to high precision 3D segmentation models. Unique contribution of PC-Seg is usage of single 2D model to learn cross-view consistency from B-scans and orthogonal slices to generate reliable volumetric (3D) pseudo-labels. These labels are then distilled into a 3D model, followed by a co-training phase where 2D and 3D models mutually refine each other through ensemble pseudo-labeling. On MSHC and Duke DME datasets, the ensemble version of proposed method outperformed five domain specific supervised methods, four domain specific unsupervised methods, and four general semi-supervised frameworks. It is significant that experiments on the MSHC dataset demonstrated that PC-Seg achieves accuracy comparable to fully supervised methods using only 0.7% of the labeled data. By my judgement proposed PC-Seg method is unique approach in attempt to handle OCT anisotropy and data scarcity. Another strength of proposed PC-Seg method is that it is model agnostic, i.e., the Res Unet model is used in the paper but five-stage curriculum learning strategy is universal.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: I studied paper carefully. I do not see any significant weakness of proposed PC-Seg method. By my judgement proposed PC-Seg method is unique approach in attempt to handle OCT anisotropy and data scarcity. The only objection is that authors neither provided link to the source code of PC-Seg nor mentioned they will provide it if the paper is accepted.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and Reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are especially encouraged by Reviewer 3’s strong endorsement. Upon acceptance, we will release our complete source code and pretrained weights. 1.Novelty: Domain-Specific Paradigm vs. General Sparse 3D SSL (Rev 1, 2) Reviewer 2’s comparison to general sparse-annotation 3D SSL methods (e.g., SGTC) overlooks a fundamental physical discrepancy. Single-Planar Annotation & The Anisotropy Trap: Existing sparse-annotation 3D SSL methods require multi-planar annotations. However, in OCT, orthogonal (Ortho) B-scans exhibit severe sparsity and low inter-slice continuity, making reliable manual annotation impractical. With only sparse single-plane 2D labels, directly applying 3D models to such anisotropic data amplifies kernel biases, causing early training collapse. PC-Seg explicitly evades this “anisotropy trap.” Its core innovation is a staged dimension-lifting curriculum that requires labels from only a single plane (standard B-scan), robustly bootstrapping 3D representations without any Ortho labels. Model-Agnosticism & Efficiency: PC-Seg is backbone-agnostic. As stated in Sect. 2.1, our preliminary experiments compared ResUNet with ViT-based architectures (e.g., SegFormer, Swin-UNet). We found that 2D/3D ResUNet achieved comparable or superior performance with significantly fewer parameters. Thus, we prioritized ResUNet for computational efficiency in clinical deployment, though our paradigm also yields consistent improvements with Transformer backbones. 2.Reproducibility & 5-Stage Pipeline Justification (Rev 1, AC) Logical Necessity: As evidenced by our ablation study (Table 1), directly co-training multiple views from the initial stage causes unreliable pseudo-labels to propagate, degrading performance. PC-Seg’s 5-stage curriculum prevents this noise accumulation and stabilizes training by progressing through 2D B-scan warm-up, Ortho adaptation, cross-teaching, 3D distillation, and mutual refinement. Switching Criteria: For fair comparison, we utilized fixed epochs for each stage (e.g., [10, 5, 5, 50, 50] for MSHC), determined through preliminary experiments, which will be specified in the revision. Additionally, stage transitions can be dynamically triggered by validation loss convergence (patience=5), significantly optimizing total training time. Implementation: 3D pseudo-labels are formed by stacking 2D probability maps. Orthogonal alignment requires only simple coordinate permutation. We evaluated thresholds $\tau \in {0.90, 0.95, 0.99}$ and found $\tau=0.95$ optimal. 3.Statistical Significance and Robustness (Rev 1, 2) To validate reliability, we report variance analysis across 7 independent trials using different random seeds for the most practical setting (MSHC 60 labels). PC-Seg consistently achieved a Dice score of 0.9175 \pm 0.0012, outperforming the strongest baseline (2D ResUNet w/ UM: 0.9123 \pm 0.0029). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test confirmed these improvements are statistically significant ($p = 0.0156$). We will update Tables 1-3 with these standard deviations. 4.Figure 1 Clarity (Rev 2) To comply with page limits, Fig. 1 emphasizes the macro-level lifting workflow. In the revision, we will significantly expand the caption to explicitly map the abstracted “Train” arrows to the underlying SSL operations (e.g., four perturbations and cross-teaching). PC-Seg provides a robust, domain-specialized solution using only single-planar supervision. We hope this response fully addresses the reviewers’ concerns and assists the Area Chairs in their final assessment.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This work received mixed reviews, with major concerns regarding its technical novelty compared with related works and the heavy design of its five-stage training pipeline. Reproducibility and model details, such as the 2D-to-3D lifting, require further clarification. In addition, the figures should be improved for better clarity. Therefore, the authors are invited to submit a rebuttal addressing these issues. | After the rebuttal, most reviewers provided positive comments and acknowledged the contribution of using 2D cues for 3D segmentation. The authors’ response regarding the motivation is convincing, particularly for OCT segmentation. Although concerns remain about the heavy framework, the superior performance demonstrates a meaningful contribution to the relevant community. Therefore, final acceptance is recommended. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After reviewing the authors’ rebuttal and the reviewers’ final recommendations, I lean on the side of rejection, primarily due to concerns regarding the novelty of the proposed approach. As noted by Reviewer 1, the method appears conceptually close to existing approaches such as SGTC, yet these related works are neither adequately discussed nor included in the experimental comparisons. The AC shares the concern that such methods could potentially be adapted to the problem setting considered in this paper, making it difficult to clearly assess the methodological contribution beyond existing literature. Consequently, the experimental validation does not sufficiently establish the distinctiveness and added value of the proposed approach. Given these concerns, the AC is unable to recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After carefully reviewing the rebuttal and the post-rebuttal reviewer comments, my recommendation is to accept the paper. The paper addresses an important and practical problem of 3D OCT segmentation under sparse 2D annotation, and proposes PC-Seg, a progressive cross-view framework that lifts limited 2D supervision into volumetric pseudo-labels through staged cross-view consistency, 2D-to-3D distillation, and 2D/3D co-training. Although the method combines several existing ideas such as cross-view consistency, pseudo-labeling, curriculum learning, and co-training, the integration is well tailored to anisotropic OCT data and is practically meaningful for reducing annotation burden. The rebuttal clarified important concerns regarding the OCT-specific motivation, staged training rationale, pseudo-label generation, orthogonal alignment, confidence thresholds, statistical analysis, and code release. While some concerns remain about novelty relative to recent sparse-annotation methods and the complexity of the multi-stage pipeline, the majority of reviewers support acceptance after rebuttal, and the empirical results appear strong under very limited annotation settings. Therefore, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors will further clarify the annotation ratios, pipeline details, and limitations in the final version.

title: Percept-Aware Surgical Planning for Visual Cortical Prostheses with Vascular Avoidance
reviewer_1_strengths: The topic is timely and relevant, and well aligned with the scope of miccai. The paper addresses a clearly defined problem and proposes a structured methodological solution. The approach is novel and sufficiently developed for a conference contribution, and the method is generally clear and reproducible. The manuscript is also well written and easy to follow overall, with a clear presentation of the main ideas.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The authors give a reasonable explanation for not using learned perceptual metrics, because phosphene images are substantially different from normal images. However, a similar concern may also apply to the use of resnet 50 for task-level evaluation, since this model is also trained on natural images. The paper should explain more clearly why this evaluation is still appropriate in this context. The claims about performance improvements are not fully consistent with the reported results. The manuscript states that percept-aware optimization “consistently reduced reconstruction error relative to both visual field tiling and visual field coverage. ” However, for cifar 10, the results show that performance is only comparable to coverage-based optimization, and in some cases does not outperform it. This inconsistency between the general claim and the reported results should be clarified or the wording should be made more precise. The claim that perceptual quality “remained largely unchanged” after introducing safety constraints is not sufficiently supported by statistical analysis. While small percentage decreases in SSIM are reported, it isn’t clear whether these differences are statistically significant. Providing appropriate statistical tests would strengthen this claim. Some aspects of the figures could also be clarified. In Fig. 2 (left), it is not clear why coverage-based results are not included in the visual comparison. In addition, the interpretation of the metrics (MSE and SSIM) is not immediately clear from the figure, as the direction of improvement (e. g. , lower is better for MSE, higher is better for SSIM) is not explicitly indicated. This makes the comparison somewhat difficult to interpret. In Section 4.3, the description of “threaded arrays” is unclear, as the concept is not sufficiently explained earlier in the manuscript. A brief definition or reference to the device design would help the reader understand what is being optimized. In addition, methodological aspects such as the optimization setup (e. g. , the choice of N_insert = 128) appear in the results section without prior explanation, which makes the structure difficult to follow. These design choices should be introduced and justified in the methods section, while the results section should focus on reporting outcomes. There are also inconsistencies between the Results and Discussion sections. The Discussion states that percept-aware placement “consistently improved reconstruction fidelity relative to coverage-based strategies,” whereas the Results indicate that performance relative to coverage-based optimization depends on the dataset (e. g. , comparable performance on CIFAR-10 rather than consistent improvement). In addition, tiling-based baselines are not mentioned in the Discussion, despite being part of the main comparison in the Results. The Discussion should more accurately reflect the reported findings.

title: Physics-Based iOCT Sonification for Real-Time Interaction Awareness in Subretinal Injection
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The system employs a two-dimensional mass-spring-damper acoustic model anchored to anatomical segmentations. 2.The full processing pipeline operates at approximately 36 FPS, ensuring it is compatible with interactive surgical workflows. 3.The framework showed particular strength in identifying subretinal bleb formation, with a 21.8% point increase in identification accuracy over the baseline.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.the accuracy for identifying the most critical safety boundaries showed only minor improvements or even slight declines. 2.Since damage to the RPE is irreversible and a primary concern in this surgery, the lack of robust improvement in this specific area is a limitation. 3.The physical parameters (mass, stiffness, damping) for the sound model are hand-crafted based on anatomical class labels and intensity statistics. These fixed mappings might not account for patient-specific variations in tissue properties, such as differences in retinal stiffness or thickness due to disease states.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: A major strength of the paper is that it addresses a clearly defined clinical problem in a procedure where the safety margin is extremely small. The manuscript explains that the macular retina is only about 250 µm thick on average and that the RPE lies directly beneath the target and has very limited regenerative capacity, which makes precise depth control essential during subretinal injection. The proposed use of sonification is therefore well motivated, because current workflows require surgeons to interpret both the en face microscope view and a cross sectional iOCT stream during a critical insertion phase, which can increase cognitive load and divide attention. Another major strength is that the method is not only conceptually interesting but also supported by concrete results. The framework uses a physics inspired mass spring damper sound model tied to segmented ILM, retina, RPE, and needle geometry, and explicitly incorporates deformation aware cues rather than only static proximity information. In the user study with 34 analyzed participants, the proposed method improved overall event identification from 60.6% to 83.4% and showed its largest gain in bleb detection, improving from 63.6% to 85.5% with p < 0.001.The full system also ran in 27.8 ± 1.5 ms per frame, about 36 FPS, which supports its practical feasibility for real time use.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: A major weakness is that the evaluation stops at event identification accuracy rather than showing impact on the actual procedure. The user study demonstrates improved recognition of ILM contact, RPE contact, and bleb onset, but it does not test whether sonification improves needle placement, reduces overshoot, lowers RPE injury risk, or improves subretinal injection success during a realistic task. Therefore, the current evidence supports perceptual usefulness, but not yet clinical performance benefit. A second weakness is that the method depends heavily on segmentation and hand crafted sonification design choices, but robustness is not analyzed in enough detail. The framework uses a pre trained U-Net, confidence weighted spline fitting, and a manual mapping from anatomical class and intensity to physical sound parameters, yet there is little quantitative discussion of how segmentation errors, missed layer boundaries, or parameter choices affect the final audio output. The expert assessment is also based on only 4 participants, which is too limited to draw strong conclusions about intraoperative usability.

reviewer_3_strengths: The real-time system aspect together with the user study are positive points.

title: PhysOCT: Physics-Guided Retinal Modeling for OCT Image Synthesis
reviewer_1_strengths: S1.The paper addresses an important limitation of OCT synthesis methods: the lack of explicit anatomical and physical constraints. While purely data-driven generative models may implicitly capture these constraints, there is no guarantee that anatomical consistency will be imposed in practice. The proposed method addresses this issue by explicitly enforcing deformation consistency through a physics-guided prior. S2.The paper proposes an interesting combination of a physics-based deformation model with a deep generative framework. The use of a physically consistent warped OCT B-scan as a conditioning signal is conceptually simple but effective, according to the experiments. S3.The method leverages the differentiability of the physical solver to learn a mapping from lesion evolution (represented as fluid masks) to the solver inputs in an end-to-end manner. This enables the integration of high-level, image-based signals with a physics-based deformation model. While similar ideas have been explored in differentiable simulation frameworks (e. g. , DiffTaichi), their application to retinal OCT deformation from fluid lesions, together with integration into generative modeling, is interesting and potentially extensible. S4.The proposed method shows consistent improvements in deformation prediction accuracy and image synthesis quality across different datasets and generative backbones. This suggests that the approach may be broadly applicable.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: W1.My main concern with this paper is conceptual and relates to the practical usefulness of the proposed approach. While the motivation of improving synthetic OCT generation under limited data is clear, the proposed method relies on existing OCT B-scans and their corresponding fluid annotations as inputs to synthesize future B-scans. This already limits the diversity of the generated data, as it remains inherently tied to the available labeled dataset, a limitation that does not arise in purely data-driven generative models. This limitation becomes more pronounced as the method additionally requires the fluid mask not only at time t, but also at time t+1 in order to synthesize the future image. In practice, fluid masks are obtained as annotations (or segmentation maps) of OCT images, and it is therefore unclear in which scenarios one would have access to a realistic mask at time t+1 without already having the corresponding OCT scan. If such a scan is already available, the need to estimate the deformation through PhysOCT appears less compelling, as one could directly use the observed image to condition the generative model. A possible alternative would be to generate plausible future fluid masks. However, in order to meet the constraints assumed by the method, this would itself require modeling the fluid masks under anatomical and physical constraints, which is a non-trivial problem and is not addressed in the paper. Overall, these limitations suggest that the method may have limited capacity to generate substantially new samples, making its practical impact for data augmentation or training data generation unclear. W2.While the proposed method shows consistent improvements over baseline generative models in terms of image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, FID), it remains unclear how these gains translate into practical benefits for image analysis tasks. In particular, the evaluation does not assess the impact of the generated data on downstream applications, such as segmentation or disease estimation, which are ultimately the relevant use cases in the MICCAI context. Improvements in image quality and fidelity metrics do not necessarily imply that the images serve as more useful training data or will help to improve the downstream task. In some cases, overly clean or highly constrained images may even reduce variability and limit generalization, while diverse, potentially noisy samples (including less physically consistent ones) can be beneficial for training and prevent overfitting. From a practical perspective, it is therefore unclear whether the additional complexity and computational cost of generating physically plausible deformations leads to measurable improvements in downstream performance. More generally, and related to W1, it would be important to compare the proposed approach with purely data-driven generative models that do not rely on labeled inputs. While such models may lack explicit physical consistency, they can potentially generate a larger variety of samples, which may lead to improved downstream performance. This aspect is not explored in the current experimental evaluation. W3.The training procedure for the force prediction network is not fully clear, particularly regarding the correspondence between sampled points across time steps. The method samples a set of points x_i^t from the retinal area at time t, which are then deformed using the predicted forces to obtain their estimated positions at time t+1.The loss (Equation (2)) is defined by comparing these deformed positions of the points at time t with positions x_i^{t+1} of the points sampled at the next time step t+1. However, it is not clear how the correspondence between the points at times t and t+1 is established. The description and Figure 1 suggest that point sampling is performed independently at each time step based on the retinal region, without relying on a predefined deformation or tracking mechanism. In such a case, there is no obvious one-to-one mapping between the sampled points at t and those at t+1 used as ground truth. In fact, the number of points sampled at t and at t+1 does not even need to be the same. Since Equation (2) assumes a pointwise correspondence with N points (same for t and t+1), it would be important to clarify how this matching is performed in practice. This detail is critical for understanding the training procedure and ensuring reproducibility. W4.[Minor] The physical interpretation of the learned force field remains somewhat unclear. In particular, multiple point-wise force configurations can be projected to the same kernel-level forces (via the projection of Eq. (1)). Therefore, the predicted forces may not directly correspond to meaningful biomechanical quantities. Instead, they may act as latent variables (as opposed to physical forces) that parameterize deformation within the solver. While this does not necessarily limit the effectiveness of the method, it suggests that PhysOCT could be better understood as a physics-inspired regularization approach rather than a model of physically accurate forces. It would be interesting (but not critical) to visualize the estimated point-wise forces in a few cases to better assess their plausibility. In any case, I do not consider this to be a major issue with the method.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The technical innovation is well motivated and conceptually novel. The paper introduces a new perspective on OCT synthesis by formulating lesion evolution as a differentiable physical deformation process, thereby enabling the derivation of physically interpretable structural priors for OCT B-scan generation. 2.The methodology of PhysOCT is mathematically grounded and insightful. The framework estimates generalized forces from point-wise forces via the principle of virtual work, and then simulates retinal geometry through a differentiable solver, resulting in physically grounded conditions for reliable OCT generation. 3.Extensive experiments on diverse disease(AMD/CNV/DME) OCT images and two major generation framworks(DDPM and LDM) further demonstrate its improvement and generalizability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There are also several weaknesses of this manuscript: 1.The major weaknesses is the incomplete disclosure of dataset size, especially for the private CNV cohort. 2.The paper’s claims would benefit from a more rigorous justification through ablation studies on image generation conditions. Although the experimental results are relatively self-contained from the physical simulation perspective，the generation pipeline in PhysOCT involves multiple inputs, including the warped OCT sketch, the predicted layer prior, and the target fluid structure. Since the target fluid mask may provide a strong structural prior for image generation, disentangling the contribution of each conditioning signal would help clarify the performance gains and make the paper’s claims more convincing. 3.The presentation of Table 2 has the potential to be misleading. The entries “100× parameters” and “0.01× parameters” appear to correspond to a sensitivity analysis of the Young’s modulus E, but this is not explicitly specified in the table and may cause ambiguity for readers. Since the simulation relies on the point-wise discretization of the retinal layers, a further sensitivity analysis with respect to the sampled points numer N would substantially improve the transparency of the method. 4.In practice, the training of PhysOCT still relies on point-level supervision extracted from the target-layer for the force predictor. As such, the claim that the method operates “without dense paired structural supervision at scale” may require further clarification and more explicit justification. 5.Including downstream utility validation, such as evaluating the anatomical consistency between generated images and the ground truth or assessing the diagnostic performance of models trained on the synthesized data, would further enhance the rigor of the study and better demonstrate its practical value. 6.The authors should also discuss the limitations of the proposed method. For example, under what circumstances would this method fail?
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Novel hybrid formulation: It bridges neural networks and biomechanics by predicting lesion-induced point-wise forces and propagating them through a physics solver to ensure anatomically consistent layer deformations 2.Modular Architecture: PhysOCT is designed as a flexible conditioner that integrates with existing diffusion models to improve generation fidelity. 3.Stable Differentiable Solver: The framework ensures stable end-to-end training by predicting point-wise forces and utilizing an SPD linear system to avoid numerical failures. 4.Efficient: It provides minimal computational overhead 5.Evaluated thoroughly for MICCAI standards on three different longitudinal disease datasets (CNV, DME and AMD).
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Fixed biomechanical parameters: Tissue elasticity may vary widely between individual patients and age groups - though I understand that this is needed for now for numerical stability. 2.Limitation to 2D: I understand that this is mainly due to a computational barrier, yet I want to mention it: Currently it is strictly limited into 2D, by predicting 2D forces, but this ignores crucial out-of-plane forces, which are present in the three dimensional retinal volumes. 3.No comparison against SOTA generative models, like SD3, FLUX. Minor comments: Please use vector graphics wherever it is possible. The plots in Figure 2 and Figure 3 are currently rasterized, which do not look so nice. Also, if possible, please include the full-scale images in the work (downscaled only in PDF), so that upon zooming in, the small details become visible. I find this very important for publications about generative models.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: Thank all reviewers and the AC for their constructive feedback. We address the main concerns below. (1) R1-W1, Meta-Reviewer: Concern that the method requires a real t+1 scan, limiting practical utility. PhysOCT is positioned as a physics-consistent OCT image editing model, not an image predictor. At inference, the t+1 fluid mask comes from: (i) clinician-specified or algorithmically edited fluid masks derived from a known mask, e.g., augmenting rare lesion morphologies (similar to FESM [20]); (ii) a mask prediction network, which addresses a lower-dimensional structure prediction task than full-image synthesis. In both cases, no real t+1 scan exists or is necessary. PhysOCT’s core value lies in turning a mask-level edit into an anatomically consistent image edit, a guarantee that purely data-driven generators cannot provide. (2) Meta-Reviewer, R3-W2: Concern about the method’s 2D limitation and extensibility to 3D. The formulation extends naturally to 3D: both the physics simulator and force prediction can be lifted to 3D. The main obstacles are computational cost and the scarcity of paired longitudinal OCT volumes. A 2.5D extension is a feasible intermediate, with GMLS interpolation keeping the cost increase manageable. (3) R1-W3: Lack of clarity on point correspondence between t and t+1.Points at time t are uniformly sampled pixel-wise within the retinal region defined by layer_t, excluding the lesion region. At time t+1, each sampled point retains its relative position within its inter-layer band, and is mapped via linear interpolation between layer_t and layer_{t+1}. The resulting t+1 coordinates serve as supervision for the force prediction network. (4) R1-W2, R2-W5, R3: Absence of downstream task evaluation. We agree downstream evaluation is important. As R2 highlights, “anatomical consistency between generated images and ground truth” is the key evaluation axis, which is exactly what our deformation metrics (Rel-L2/MAE, Table 1) and layer-overlay analysis (Fig. 3) directly measure. Common OCT segmentation tasks (fluid or layer) are not the most sensitive probe of PhysOCT’s contribution: PhysOCT can introduce lesion/layer diversity by editing the t+1 fluid mask, but since the generated images are derived from existing scans, diversity-driven augmentation is not its strongest fit; meanwhile, the layer-lesion structural consistency that PhysOCT contributes does not directly translate into segmentation gains. A more suitable downstream task is longitudinal dataset augmentation for temporal prediction. These tasks demand high realism in predicted images, and require augmented training data anatomically realistic and physically coherent. This is exactly what PhysOCT delivers. By analyzing fluid-evolution distributions and generating under-represented trends via targeted mask editing, PhysOCT can augment longitudinal datasets in ways unattainable by appearance-based generation. (5) R2-W1: Incomplete disclosure of the CNV dataset size. The CNV cohort includes 39 patients and 49 paired longitudinal 3D cubes (Optovue, 400×640×400). 936 paired 2D B-scans with substantial lesion change are split 8:2 at the patient level. The force predictor uses this set; the generative model is additionally trained on remaining labeled paired B-scans from the same training patients. (6) R2-W2, R3-W3: Need for ablation on conditioning signals and comparison with SOTA generators. Our main contribution is the PhysOCT framework, not the backbone. Table 3 acts as the ablation: DDPM/LDM baselines use fluid_{t+1} and the current image, while +PhysOCT adds the warped sketch and layer prior, with consistent PSNR/SSIM/FID gains and boundary-aligned error reduction in Fig. 3.SD3/FLUX, as natural-image foundation models, differ from the OCT setting in both training scale and domain, making fair comparison infeasible; meanwhile, PhysOCT is designed as a pluggable module, orthogonal to backbone choice, hence our comparison focus on standard LDM/DDPM.

title: Prompt and Probe: Data-Efficient Adaptation of Black-Box Foundation Models via Unified Active Visual Prompting
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The problem statement is genuinely novel and practically motivated. The compound constraint — black-box FMs and annotation budget — is a real gap. 2.Using a shared backbone with two heads is parameter-efficient, important under SPSA where each parameter incurs query cost. The choice of ~2.1M parameters is reasonably small for zeroth-order optimization. 3.The evaluation is rigorous with seven datasets across six modalities, three task settings (C, S, joint), and 10-run statistical reporting. 4.Interesting results from the cross-task transfer which shows that spatial uncertainty is a useful signal for classification AL. 5.The query budget (with ~50k queries at 1k queries/min) is practical and clinically useful as a deployment metric.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Removing a single weighting term (w_b=0) causing a 24.5 AUROC drop on a classification-only dataset (CheXpert) is extraordinarily large. This needs more explanation given that rhe boundary disagreement signal I_bnd is computed on segmentation masks. CheXpert has no segmentation ground truth. Moreover, the mechanism by which a segmentation signal produces this magnitude of classification gain on a chest X-ray classification task is not explained. 2.L_unified is presented without weighting coefficients between L_task, L_div, L_ent, L_feat, and without explaining the balancing mechanism. 3.Refering to Fig. 3, the FSL is reported as 92.4%. However, state-of-the-art CheXpert AUROC values for the standard 5-finding evaluation are typically 0.92–0.94.Why is the FSL ceiling so low ? My guess is a weak implementation (ex. : a DenseNet121-baseline compared to a ViT-B/16 + foundation model for P^2). 4.The paper provides no description of the hyper-parameter tuning protocol (held-out validation set? cross-validation? grid search budget?). 5.The authors claim that task-unified is “fundamentally” superior given the evidence is that adding spatial signals helps classification on medical imaging benchmarks where anatomical structure correlates with diagnosis. However, this does not seem to generalize to pure classification tasks where no segmentation prior exists. The term “fundamental” appears to be the misnomer. It would be great if the authors can clarify this.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper proposes a novel Prompt and Probe (P2) framework along with a lightweight Visual Prompt Decoder to address the dual challenges of deploying foundation models in clinical imaging. Extensive experiments on seven public datasets covering six clinical modalities demonstrate that P2 reduces labeling requirements by 40–60% while matching or exceeding fully supervised baselines.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1 The paper lacks clear organization, and the writing is difficult to follow. 2 There is insufficient explanation of certain design choices, such as why addition is used in the classification branch while concatenation is used in the segmentation branch. 3 It is unclear whether Ltask and other loss functions are defined under the same scale; if not, the absence of balancing coefficients may be an issue.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: S1.Well-scoped compound problem formulation. The simultaneous constraints of API opacity and annotation scarcity are genuine deployment bottlenecks in clinical AI. The gap analysis in Section 1 is specific and accurate, clearly positioning P² against VALIANT, BAPS, ZIP, and BlackVIP along three dimensions: black-box compatibility, annotation efficiency, and cross-task unification. No prior work satisfies all three simultaneously, and the paper makes a credible case for this gap.S2.Dual-use of VIPD as both prompt generator and uncertainty instrument. Repurposing a trained prompt decoder for informativeness estimation, without additional parameters or a separate acquisition module ,is an architecturally elegant economy. This avoids the common pitfall of bolting an independent uncertainty estimator onto a prompting framework, and the design consequence (sensitivity to input characteristics is exactly what is needed for sample selection) is intellectually compelling.S3.The cross-task signal transfer finding is scientifically significant. A 24.5-point AUROC drop on CheXpert,a classification-only dataset,from removing boundary disagreement signals alone is the paper’s most striking result. If reproducible and mechanistically validated, this implies that spatial boundary uncertainty is a domain-general proxy for diagnostic ambiguity in medical images, with implications extending well beyond this framework.S4.Breadth and realism of evaluation. Eight benchmarks across six modalities with API-constraint simulation using open-source FMs with all internal access explicitly disabled (BioViL, MedCLIP, MedSAM) is methodologically responsible and unusually broad for this class of paper. This exceeds the evaluation scope of any individual prior method in this space.S5.Practical deployability signal. Reporting convergence within 0.9 pts of FSL at ~50K queries (<1h at 1K queries/min) gives practitioners concrete, actionable guidance on real-world deployment feasibility, a type of analysis absent from most AL papers in medical imaging.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: W1 [Critical]. The feature consistency loss Lfeat = ||F(X+P) − F(X)||² requires evaluation of intermediate representations F(·). Under the strict black-box constraint that defines the paper’s central premise, no access to weights, gradients, or activations, this loss cannot be computed on FM features. If F(·) refers to VIPD-internal features rather than FM features, the loss must be reframed as decoder self-regularization rather than FM feature drift constraint. As written, this is a direct contradiction of the paper’s core claim and must be explicitly resolved.W2 [Critical]. The rank fusion in Eq. 5 (RankFinal = γ·ICls + (1−γ)·ISeg) is a weighted sum of raw scores, not ranks. The abstract and body both use “rank-based fusion,” which is misleading. More substantively, ICls and ISeg are derived from different quantities (cosine dissimilarity + finite-difference sensitivity vs. pixel entropy + boundary Dice + volumetric change) and have different scales and distributions. Without normalization prior to fusion, the combined score will be dominated by the larger-magnitude component in an unpredictable, dataset-dependent manner. No normalization step is described.W3 [Significant]. The diversity loss Ldiv = −D_KL(y_prob || y^p_prob) maximizes KL divergence between original and perturbed outputs without a stabilization bound. Its interaction with the entropy term Lent which penalizes entropy proportional to prompt similarity S ,is not analyzed. When S takes intermediate values, both losses may partially oppose each other, creating unstable gradients. No loss interaction analysis or training stability curves are provided.W4 [Significant]. SPSA optimization at ~2.1M parameters raises unaddressed convergence concerns. The SPSA gradient estimator variance scales as O(d) in parameter dimensionality, making convergence noisier as parameter count grows. No variance analysis, adaptive perturbation schedule, or comparison to alternative zeroth-order methods (e.g., CMA-ES) is provided. Without convergence curves or stability analysis, the claim that zeroth-order training is “practical” at this parameter scale is asserted rather than demonstrated.W5 [Significant]. Baseline selection is inconsistent with the paper’s own threat model. Entropy Sampling is included as a black-box baseline, despite Section 1 explicitly arguing that API-served models do not expose calibrated softmax distributions. Genuinely black-box-compatible alternatives—margin sampling, least-confidence sampling, or diversity-based k-center clustering on image features requiring no FM interaction—are absent from the comparison.W6 [Significant]. The headline result (24.5 AUROC from ωb=0 on CheXpert) rests on a single dataset and single ablation condition. No sample-level analysis establishes what samples are uniquely selected by boundary disagreement, making it impossible to validate the anatomical ambiguity hypothesis against simpler explanations (e.g., CheXpert pathologies such as cardiomegaly and pleural effusion inherently involve complex organ boundaries, which may be a dataset-specific rather than universal phenomenon).W7 [Significant]. Dataset-specific tuning of 10 hyperparameters per dataset (Table 1) using a 3% stratified seed is a substantial methodological concern. The tuning procedure, whether a separate validation split was used, and whether hyperparameter selection consumed annotation budget are not described.W8 [Minor]. An unresolved “Fig. ??” cross-reference appears in Section 3.The abstract cites 92.8% AUROC on CheXpert with 60% labels, but the body reports 91.8% at 50% and 97.6% at 100%—the 92.8% figure is not traceable to any table or figure in the main text. Reference [3] (VALIANT, AAAI 2026, cited anonymously) appears to be prior work from the same group; the incremental technical contribution over VALIANT is not clearly delineated.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers for recognizing P2’s compound-problem framing, the dual-use VIPD design, evaluation breadth, and the cross-task transfer finding. [R1.1/R3.6] CheXpert +24.5 AUROC mechanism. Critical clarification: I_bnd uses NO segmentation GT. At probe time, MedSAM produces predicted boundary maps for the unlabeled CXR (original and perturbed); I_bnd = 1 - Dice(boundary_orig, boundary_pert) measures instability of MedSAM’s own predictions. Mechanism: CheXpert pathologies (cardiomegaly, effusion, atelectasis) have diagnostically informative contours; unstable boundaries indicate ambiguous anatomy, correlated with classification ambiguity. ~62% of I_bnd-uniquely-selected samples carry one of these labels (vs. ~31% base rate) — real cross-task transfer, not supervision leakage. [R1.2/R2.3] L_unified weighting. Each term is naturally bounded — L_task is CE/Dice; L_div, L_ent in ~[0, log K]; L_feat is Lipschitz-bounded on the small VIPD trunk. All four stay within 1.5x of each other through training; no manual coefficient needed (curves added). [R1.3] FSL ceiling. FSL 92.4% uses ViT-B/16 with matched preprocessing and 5-finding eval — within the 0.92-0.94 ViT range. DenseNet-121 is a textual reference, not the FSL backbone. [R1.4/R3.7] Hyperparameter protocol. The 3% stratified seed is the validation split; tuning is random search over 30 trials per dataset, held out from the labeled pool — selection does NOT consume annotation budget. [R1.5] “Fundamentally” overstated. Agreed — replaced with “consistently superior in the medical-imaging setting evaluated”. [R1.6] Statistical test. Paired t-test over 10 runs with Bonferroni correction across all comparisons. [R1.7] Tab.2 ACDC inconsistency. “Ours” uses dataset-specific weights (Tab.1) on top of (alpha_1, gamma); “Equal” fixes ALL weights uniformly. Caption clarified. [R1.8/R3.8] Fig.??/Ref.[3]/ abstract. Cross-refs fixed; abstract 92.8% is P2 at 60% labels (Fig.3). VALIANT delta: it is classification-only black-box AL; P2 adds unified global+spatial prompting from one decoder, segmentation, and cross-task acquisition. [R3.1] L_feat black-box consistency. Wording bug: F(.) is the VIPD’s OWN MLP-trunk feature (shared 1024-d activation), not FM features. L_feat = ||F_VIPD(X+P) - F_VIPD(X)||^2 is decoder self-regularization; no FM internals accessed. Renamed to L_self. [R3.2] Score normalization. Per-batch min-max (“rank-based” = the resulting ranking): I_hat = (I - min_B)/(max_B - min_B + eps); Rank = gamma I_hat_Cls + (1-gamma) I_hat_Seg. Kvasir@10% Dice / CheXpert@50% AUROC: raw 56.8 / 90.6; min-max 58.5 / 91.8 (reported); Borda-rank 58.2 / 91.7.Eq. 5 corrected. [R3.3] L_div / L_ent interaction. L_div’s KL is bounded by the supervised-loss-anchored perturbation; L_ent’s S-weighting routes entropy to whichever output matches current prompt similarity—complementary, not opposed. Training-loss std < 0.03 after epoch 20.[R3.4] SPSA convergence at 2.1M params. Variance controlled via Rademacher perturbations, Spall decay c_t=c_0/t^0.101, Polyak-Ruppert momentum, and n=8 SPSA/step (~8x reduction). CheXpert (queries/AUROC/std over 10 seeds): 5K : 71.3 / 2.1 10K : 82.4 / 1.4 20K : 88.1 / 0.8 50K : 91.5 / 0.5 100K : 91.8 / 0.4 Std contracts monotonically. CMA-ES at matched budget: 3-5 AUROC worse, ~3x memory. [R3.5] Baselines under strict black-box. Entropy Sampling assumes returned probabilities (open-source FMs comply); caveat stated. Added strictly black-box baselines (CheXpert@50% / Kvasir@10%): Random : 84.2 / 45.0 K-Center : 85.7 / 47.3 Coreset(CLIP) : 87.1 / 49.8 Margin : 88.4 / 51.2 Entropy : 88.9 / 52.6 P2 (Ours) : 91.8 / 58.5 [R2.1] Sec. 2 will be tightened with a notation table. [R2.2] Add vs. concat. Classification uses additive prompts because z_I is a fixed-dim semantic vector—additive fusion preserves geometry without expanding FM input. Segmentation needs spatial alignment, so the spatial prompt is channel-concatenated.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I am weighing the R2 accept with a lesser coefficient, and, thus, sending paper for the rebuttal. title: Proto-CAP: Prototype Memory Fusion and Curriculum-Adaptive Loss for Pediatric Myopia Visual Question Answering
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper studies a clinically meaningful problem. Pediatric myopia is important in practice, and the Med-VQA setting is relevant and well-motivated. The dataset effort is valuable. PM-VQA appears to be a carefully curated multimodal dataset with expert-verified QA pairs collected from clinical data. The proposed method is reasonably matched to the task. Both the prototype-based fusion and the adaptive loss are motivated by the challenges of small-scale medical VQA. The paper includes comparisons with several baselines, ablation studies, and qualitative examples. The writing is generally clear. The overall pipeline is clear, and the qualitative visualizations help illustrate the intuition behind the method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: My main concern is the data split protocol. The paper says the data are split into train/validate/test QA pairs, but it is unclear whether the split is image-based or patient-based. Since multiple QA pairs may come from the same image, this should be clarified carefully. Table 2 needs stronger justification. Some compared methods are not sufficiently introduced, and it is therefore unclear why these baselines were selected. It would also strengthen the paper to compare with a more recent Med-VQA method, or at least discuss the difference more explicitly. There are two issues about Table 3.First, why are Accuracy and Recall exactly the same for every row? If this is expected due to the metric definition, please explain it clearly. Second, Precision drops when either Proto or CAP is added alone, but improves when both are combined. The paper should give a clearer explanation of this interaction. The contribution of the proposed loss needs to be clarified further. Its formulation appears closely related to PolyLoss [1], but the current presentation does not make it clear what the substantive difference is and why the proposed variant is necessary in this setting. The paper would benefit from more details on the dataset and implementation. For example, it would be helpful to report the number of patients, the distribution of question types, whether all samples contain all modalities, and several missing training details needed to fully understand the setup. [1]. Leng, Z. , Tan, M. , Liu, C. , Cubuk, E. D. , Shi, X. , Cheng, S. , & Anguelov, D. (2022). PolyLoss: A polynomial expansion perspective of classification loss functions [Preprint]. arXiv. doi:10.48550/arXiv. 2204.12511
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Important application setting. Pediatric myopia is clinically relevant, and Med-VQA for this disease is underexplored. The paper addresses a meaningful real-world problem. Potentially useful dataset contribution. PM-VQA fills a gap in multimodal ophthalmic Med-VQA. If publicly released with clear protocols, it could become a useful benchmark for future work. Reasonable method design. The prototype fusion and adaptive loss are both well motivated for small-scale medical data, and the method is easy to understand. Clear empirical presentation. The paper includes baseline comparisons, ablations, and qualitative examples, which make the proposed improvements easy to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The method novelty is limited. The proposed Prototype Memory Fusion mainly combines prototype/memory learning, question-guided attention, and gated fusion, which are all familiar ideas in vision-language and medical multimodal learning. The paper does not clearly explain what is fundamentally new beyond adapting these components to this task. A similar concern applies to the Curriculum-Adaptive Poly-2 Loss. Dynamic reweighting, curriculum learning, and hard-sample emphasis have all been widely studied, so the current loss design appears incremental rather than conceptually novel. The paper should better position itself relative to prior work on memory/prototype learning and adaptive losses. Relevant references include Bengio et al. (2009), Santoro et al. (2016), Snell et al. (2017), Sukhbaatar et al. (2015), Lin et al. (2017), and Leng et al. (2022). The experimental validation is still limited. The reported gains over MMQL are promising but relatively modest, and all results are shown only on the newly introduced PM-VQA dataset. There is no external validation on another Med-VQA benchmark. The paper also does not report variance, confidence intervals, or repeated runs with different random seeds. On a relatively small medical dataset, such reporting is important to show that the improvements are stable. In addition, comparisons are mainly against prior Med-VQA baselines, but there is limited discussion of stronger modern multimodal baselines or pretrained vision-language models. This makes the “state-of-the-art” claim somewhat less convincing. The paper’s value depends heavily on whether the dataset will be released. In my view, the dataset is the most impactful part of the submission. However, the paper is not sufficiently clear about whether PM-VQA will be publicly released, and if so, under what access conditions.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1- Pediatric myopia is a major public-health issue (cited prevalence of ~50% of the world’s population by 2050). Existing Med-VQA benchmarks (VQA-RAD [7], SLAKE [12]) are radiology-centric, while existing ophthalmology VQA datasets (DME-VQA [19], INSEGCAT-VQA [20], OphthalWeChat [22]) are largely repurposed from public datasets, single-modality, or lack QA verification (Table 1). PM-VQA is the only entry that is simultaneously clinical-source, multimodal (CFP+OCT) and QA-verified, which is a real value-add for the community. 2- QA pairs are formulated by two ophthalmologists and re-validated by a senior expert, with explicit quality control and de-identification stages (Fig. 1). Ethics committee approval is reported. This is stronger annotation governance than most ophthalmology VQA datasets. 3- The Prototype Memory Fusion is a sensible inductive bias for small-scale medical data: parameterising medical concepts as a learnable memory addresses the well-known data-scarcity problem cited in the introduction. The gating mechanism preserves the original visual stream, mitigating the risk that the prototype path overrides image evidence — a nice design choice. The Curriculum-Adaptive Poly-2 Loss is a clean, lightweight extension of Poly-Loss [8] that ties coefficient scheduling to a model-state signal (accuracy). The cosine-decay / linear-increase schedule for e₁ / e₂ is consistent with the easy-to-hard curriculum intuition. 4- Seven Med-VQA baselines are compared (CMSA, M-Mixup, M2I2, MUMC, MEVF-BAN, Surgical-VQA, MMQL). The improvement over the closest baseline (MMQL) is non-trivial (+2.10% accuracy, +2.14% F1). 5- Table 3 ablates Proto and CAP independently and jointly, supporting the claim that the two modules are complementary (each adds something on its own; the combination is super-additive in F1: +0.98 + +0.74 individually vs +2.14 jointly). 6- The qualitative attention-map comparison in Fig. 3 (right panel) shows visibly more focal attention for Proto-CAP than for MMQL, lending some plausibility to the ‘medical-prior injection’ interpretation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1- Each component is a thin variation on prior art: The Prototype Memory Fusion is structurally a memory-augmented attention bank with a sigmoid gate. Memory networks for medical image analysis and gated text-conditioned visual fusion are well-established (e.g., dynamic memory networks for VQA, gated multimodal units of Arevalo et al. 2017, conditional reasoning of MEVF-BAN [23] which is itself a baseline here). The paper does not articulate what is fundamentally new beyond combining a learnable memory bank with a BERT-pooled query and a sigmoid gate. The Curriculum-Adaptive Poly-2 Loss is a parameter-scheduling modification of Poly-Loss [8]. The schedules for e₁ (cosine decay) and e₂ (linear increase) are not formally specified (no equations, no hyperparameters, no sensitivity analysis). Tying loss weights to training accuracy is a small step beyond [8], and self-paced / curriculum-driven loss-shaping has a long history (Kumar et al. 2010; Bengio et al. 2009; focal-loss family). Without an explicit comparison against vanilla Poly-Loss with tuned static (e₁,e₂), the added value of the adaptive aspect is not isolated. Overall the framework is MMQL [1] + memory bank + scheduled Poly-Loss; the +2.10% gain is real but modest and may largely come from the prototype module rather than from a conceptual breakthrough. 2- Table 1 advertises PM-VQA as multimodal (CFP and OCT), and the introduction motivates the work by the need for joint CFP/OCT analysis. However, Section 3 describes only a single image I processed by one Swin Transformer, with no explanation of how CFP and OCT are jointly fed to the model, aligned per-patient, or fused across modalities. Are CFP and OCT treated as independent samples (in which case the model is monomodal at inference time)? Are they concatenated, encoded by separate branches, or paired per patient? This is the most important methodological gap of the paper given that multimodality is an explicit selling point. Without clarification, the ‘multimodal’ claim is not supported by the method. 3- All experiments are run on the authors’ own PM-VQA. There is no evaluation on existing ophthalmology VQA datasets (DME-VQA, INSEGCAT-VQA, OphthalWeChat) nor on radiology benchmarks (VQA-RAD, SLAKE) to demonstrate that the Proto and CAP modules generalise. Given the reliance on a domain-specific memory bank, it is particularly important to show whether the gains transfer or whether they are tied to PM-VQA-specific concepts. 4- Tables 2 and 3 report single-point estimates with no standard deviation, no confidence interval, no multi-seed runs and no statistical test. With +2.10% accuracy on a 2,223-QA test set, the naive 95% Wilson CI for a binomial proportion is roughly ±1.7%, so the claimed gain over MMQL is barely outside the noise floor. For the Proto-only variant (+1.18%) and CAP-only variant (+0.65%) the claim is statistically not supported by the evidence shown. 5- The dataset section omits information that is essential to assess scientific value and risk of bias: Number of unique patients (vs. number of images). Patient demographics (age range, sex distribution, ethnicity, spherical-equivalent distribution, axial-length distribution). Question type taxonomy and answer space (open vs. closed; answer-vocabulary size; class imbalance). Inter-annotator agreement between the two ophthalmologists and the senior expert (Cohen’s κ or analogous). Image-level metadata (device manufacturer, resolution, OCT scan pattern), which affects external validity. How CFP and OCT are paired per patient and per QA pair. Train/val/test split protocol is it patient-level (no leakage) or QA-pair-level (likely leakage)? This is critical because many QA pairs share an image; QA-level random splitting would let the model see the same image at train and test time.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Our CAP loss mimics the clinical training process. In the early stage, when accuracy is low, e1 promotes rapid convergence, allowing the model to quickly learn fundamental and typical ophthalmic anatomical structures. The cosine schedule provides slow initial decay, accelerated mid-stage adjustment, and smooth final convergence, preventing premature or overly rapid gradient decay and reducing training instability. In the later stage, as model proficiency improves, e2 increases linearly, suppressing redundant gradients from easy samples while amplifying attention to difficult clinical cases. Unlike PolyLoss, which usually provides only marginal gains on large-scale datasets, our dynamic curriculum plays a critical role in preventing overfitting in small-scale medical data. Proto provides clinically informative high-dimensional features, while CAP offers a dynamic learning path to fully exploit these features. CAP can therefore be regarded as an enhancement to Proto, and their combination significantly outperforms either module alone.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces a pediatric myopia medical VQA benchmark (PM-VQA) and a Proto-CAP framework that combines prototype memory fusion with a curriculum-adaptive loss to improve multimodal reasoning performance. The work addresses a clinically meaningful and underexplored problem, and the curated, expert-verified dataset together with consistent empirical improvements over prior Med-VQA baselines make it potentially valuable to the community. On the other side, the reviewers also raise main concerns. First, the evaluation protocol needs clarification: the current QA-level split raises potential leakage issues, and the absence of multi-seed results, statistical testing, and robustness analysis makes the reported gains hard to judge. Second, the “multimodal” aspect is unclear, as the paper does not explain how CFP and OCT are jointly modeled or fused. Third, the novelty appears limited, with both the prototype memory and adaptive loss being incremental extensions without clear differentiation from prior work. Fourth, the empirical validation is somewhat limited: it relies on a single internal dataset, includes insufficient comparison to stronger or more recent baselines, lacks robustness and statistical analysis, and does not demonstrate whether the proposed modules generalize beyond PM-VQA. Finally, key dataset and reproducibility details are missing, weakening transparency and rigor. | This paper proposes Proto-CAP, a pediatric myopia Med-VQA framework with prototype memory fusion and curriculum-adaptive loss, together with PM-VQA, an expert-verified pediatric myopia dataset from CFP and OCT images. The main strength of the work lies in the dataset contribution: pediatric myopia Med-VQA is clinically meaningful and underexplored, and PM-VQA could provide a valuable community benchmark. title: Prototype Learning for Visual Field Estimation from Fundus Photography in High Myopia
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem. Functional assessment in high myopia is important, and the motivation for reducing dependence on subjective perimetry is well stated. The prototype-based formulation is conceptually interesting. Recasting VF estimation as coefficient prediction over a lower-dimensional prototype space is a reasonable way to impose structure and may improve interpretability. The manuscript includes both quantitative and qualitative evaluation, as well as an ablation over prototype generation methods and prototype number. That is helpful for understanding the method’s internal design choices.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1-The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior fundus-to-VF estimation work in high myopia. 2-The experimental comparison is limited. The main baseline is a generic regression model, and stronger recent high-myopia-specific methods are cited but not clearly compared in a fair, detailed way. 3- (important) I couldn’t understand how the prototypes and coefficients from the fundus images are computed. Providing pseudocode for both the training and testing phases would help clarify this. 4-Clinical validation is modest. The study is single-center, from a relatively homogeneous population, and restricted to non-glaucomatous HM (i think), which narrows the clinical significance and generalizability of the findings.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The advantage of this approach lies in transforming the parameter learning of 52 distinct point locations into the learning of lower-dimensional and more interpretable weights associated with classical visual field sensitivity distribution patterns. A particularly interesting aspect of the paper is the detailed ablation study regarding the number prototypes for visual field reports. It clearly and intuitively demonstrates the relationship between the number of prototypes and the Mean Squared Error (MSE) across different methods for generating prototypes.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: a. In the visualization of prototypes, this paper utilizes AA instead of PCA, which demonstrates superior comprehensive performance. This weakens the credibility of the conclusions. b. Neural network learning is also a crucial component. The paper lacks a theoretical justification for the network selection. It is recommended to supplement with ablation studies to elaborate on this choice. c. The conclusions related to visualization should not be placed in Section 3.4 ablation study. d. The ablation study section in Figure 3 shows that for most methods (e.g., PCA), the model accuracy improves as the number of prototypes increases. A sufficient justification is not provided for the selection of k = 10 (the paper mentions this configuration provided a favorable balance between representational capacity and generalization. But this only applies to the AA method ).
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The authors clearly stated that the training and test datasets are separated at the subject level during cross-validation. This is an important methodological practice in machine learning, as it helps prevent information leakage caused by strong correlations between paired eyes from the same individual.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Predicting HVF outcomes from color fundus photographs in highly myopic eyes is inherently challenging. Unlike glaucoma, high myopia often lacks clearly localized or easily interpretable retinal nerve fiber bundle defects in fundus images that can be directly associated with VF loss. In this context, OCT may provide more direct and informative structural indicators of optic nerve damage to support structure–function modeling and VF prediction. [However, high myopia can introduce substantial retinal curvature, which may degrade OCT image quality and lead to unreliable RNFL segmentation and thickness measurements, creating an additional source of uncertainty.] Anyway, relying solely on color fundus images represents a difficult problem setting and may limit the achievable prediction performance. In addition, the neural network architecture appears relatively conventional and may not reflect more recent advances in model design. Finally, some of the clinical background statements, such as ‘Deep learning-based estimation of VF sensitivity from fundus photography has emerged as a promising alternative; …’ appear somewhat overstated given the current limitations and variability in this task.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing the value of our work: clinical relevance, described as a “clinically meaningful problem” (R1) and an “important and challenging problem” (R3) with “innovative significance” (R2). methodological value, including a “conceptually interesting” prototype formulation to “impose structure and improve interpretability” (MR/R1), “more interpretable weights” (R2), and “quantitative and qualitative evaluation” (R1) with a “detailed ablation study” (R2). Q1: We have released anonymized GitHub code and implementation details following MICCAI reproducibility guidance. Q2 (MR/R1/R2/R3): Novelty, comparisons, and network choice ProtoVF is the first prototype-based method for VF estimation. Instead of directly regressing 52 VF sensitivities, ProtoVF predicts coefficients over a compact VF basis learned from real VF data, constraining outputs to empirically observed patterns. Thus, the contribution of ProtoVF is not a new backbone, but a structured output-space formulation for VF estimation. Our primary baseline uses the same image encoder (widely used ResNet) and training protocol, differing only in output formulation, which isolates the effect of the proposed prototype parameterization. Broader network selection is complementary to ProtoVF and does not undermine this controlled conclusion. Our results also show favorable performance relative to previous myopia-specific AI studies (Ref. 26, 27). Q3 (MR/R1): Prototype and coefficient learning We clarify that ProtoVF does not extract prototypes from fundus images. Prototypes are learned only from the training VF data. As described in Section 2.2, the prototype generator derives a fixed VF basis that provides an empirically constrained output space, while the ResNet learns image-derived coefficients over this basis. Q4 (R2): Prototype visualization and number selection Among all ProtoVFs, ProtoVF-PCA achieved the best predictive performance. The visualization, however, was intended for disease-related VF pattern analysis rather than model selection. We visualized AA because its archetypes represent boundary patterns in the VF distribution and resemble realistic, interpretable VF maps. By contrast, PCA components represent orthogonal directions of variance and are less naturally interpreted as standalone VF maps. Fig. 3 reports VF reconstruction accuracy, not final fundus-to-VF estimation accuracy. Larger k (more prototypes) reduces reconstruction error for NMF/PCA/SVD, but also requires the image encoder to infer more coefficients and may capture VF label noise. Thus, k = 10 was used as a compact operating point balancing representation and learnability. Q5 (MR/R1/R3): Imaging modality and study population R3’s concern reflects the challenge of fundus-based VF estimation in high myopia, but this does not mean fundus images lack VF-relevant structural signal. Prior clinical studies (Ref. 21, 24) reported associations between fundus morphology and VF in myopia, and previous AI studies (Ref. 26, 27) also support the feasibility of modeling this relationship. Our results provide further evidence that this signal can be learned. OCT may provide more direct structural measurements, but it is complementary rather than a replacement for our fundus-based model. Fundus photography is relatively low-cost, fast, accessible, and widely used in screening and primary-care settings. Therefore, the fundus-only setting is clinically relevant, especially for preliminary VF-risk estimation where perimetry or OCT may be unavailable. Our study is intentionally focused on high myopia, an emerging vision-threatening condition for which VF assessment is important yet often unmet and challenging (Ref. 8). However, the prototype-based output formulation is not inherently limited to high myopia and could be investigated in other diseases with structured VF loss in future work, such as glaucoma, for which characteristic VF patterns have been well documented.
