title: Reasoning Text-to-Video Retrieval for Operating Room Clips via Action-Driven Digital Twins
reviewer_1_strengths: (1) The paper introduces imagination-based retrieval, where an LLM converts the input query into a hypothetical ActDT, so that retrieval becomes an intra-modal matching problem between imagined and actual ActDTs. (2) The authors define four categories of implicit OR retrieval queries and build a dataset, which is a meaningful step toward evaluating more realistic retrieval settings in operating-room videos. (3) The paper is well organized and easy to follow. And the experimental results are thorough and detailed.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) The benchmark is promising but currently too limited. The experiments are conducted on 17 recordings, 386 clips, and 276 queries from robotic knee procedures. The dataset is relatively small for a retrieval framework that is presented as a general solution for OR reasoning retrieval. (2) The method’s novelty is meaningful but still somewhat increamental relative to very recent digital-twin-based reasoning retrieval work Reason T2V. (3) Although the large improvements on performance in Table 1, I think this is because the method benefiting from procedure-specific regularities and benchmark-specific patterns. It is unclear whether the method can generalize to larger datasets or different procedures. (4) The paper does not analyze inference efficiency, even though the proposed retrieval pipeline appears substantially more expensive than previous retrieval methods.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a meaningful retrieval problem with clear practical motivation: users often need to retrieve OR clips through implicit descriptions that depend on temporal, causal, or workflow reasoning rather than only explicit visual content. 2.The proposed action-driven digital twin representation is well aligned with this problem because it encodes subject-action-object relations over time, which is more suitable than purely object-centric descriptions for distinguishing visually similar clips. 3.The imagination-based retrieval formulation is conceptually elegant. By generating a hypothetical structured representation from the query and matching it against actual clip representations with a shared text encoder, the method reduces the cross-modal alignment gap. 4.The additional analyses on refinement, candidate-pool size, and corpus scaling are useful and go beyond a single headline result.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The benchmark is relatively small and limited to robotic knee procedures, so the broader claim of operating-room reasoning retrieval is stronger than the current evidence supports. 2.Several implementation details are missing, especially for the LLM-based generation and refinement steps. Prompting, decoding settings, metadata usage, and generation robustness are not documented well enough for reproducibility. 3.The paper relies on multiple powerful external models and repeated LLM refinement, but runtime and computational cost are not reported, which is an important omission for a practical retrieval pipeline.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A major strength is the introduction of action-driven digital twins (ActDTs). Unlike prior object-centric representations, ActDTs explicitly encode temporal action dynamics, which is crucial in surgical environments where visually similar frames differ only in interactions and procedural context
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The work builds upon existing ideas such as digital twin representations and LLM-based reasoning retrieval (e.g., ReasonT2V), with the main extension being the shift to action-driven representations and intra-modal matching. While effective, this does not constitute a fundamentally new paradigm. 2.the evaluation is limited to a single dataset and procedure type (robotic knee surgery). It remains unclear how well the method generalizes to: 1) Other surgical procedures 2) Different modalities. 3) Larger-scale datasets
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address concerns below. 1.Benchmark Scale and Generalizability (R1, R2, R3, Meta): MM-OR is currently the only public OR dataset providing both scene graph annotations and phase/step segmentation needed to construct ActDTs and implicit queries. Our benchmark of 276 queries over 386 clips covers four reasoning categories with queries authored and cross-verified by two domain-expert annotators. OR3 uses no procedure-specific rules: the ActDT vocabulary, imagination prompts, and refinement logic are derived from generic OR metadata. To test generalizability across procedures (R1, R3), we applied OR3 trained on knee surgery to 48 clips from laparoscopic cholecystectomy in CholecT50, adapting only the entity and action vocabularies. OR3 achieves 41.3% R@1 on 32 temporal/procedural queries vs. 18.8% for ReasonT2V, confirming cross-procedure transfer. Regarding different modalities (R3), ActDT construction relies on RGB frames from room-mounted cameras, which is the standard capture modality across OR datasets (e.g., MM-OR, 4D-OR, CholecT50). Extending to endoscopic views requires only swapping the VLM and segmentation models, as the ActDT structure and downstream retrieval pipeline remain unchanged. We will include these discussions in the revision. 2.Novelty Relative to ReasonT2V (R1, R3, Meta): OR3 differs from ReasonT2V in three orthogonal dimensions, each validated by ablation (Tab.2). First, ActDT replaces per-frame object listings with temporally structured action primitives grouping concurrent interactions under non-overlapping intervals. Removing ActDT causes 15.2% R@1 drop, exceeding the 9.0% gap between ReasonT2V and the best embedding baseline. Second, imagination-based retrieval is a new paradigm with no counterpart in ReasonT2V: an LLM generates a hypothetical ActDT so retrieval becomes intra-modal matching with a single encoder, eliminating paired cross-modal encoders (12.1% contribution). Third, evidence-grounded refinement revises the imagined representation itself rather than invoking specialist models to fill gaps (7.6% contribution). These are distinct design choices whose combined effect yields 33.4 R@1 points over ReasonT2V. 3.Inference Efficiency (R1, R2, Meta): We provide runtime analysis per query, averaged over the test set on a single RTX 4090.ActDT construction is offline and one-time: 38.2s per clip (VLM 24.1s, SAM-3 9.6s, depth 4.5s). At query time, imagination takes 1.8s (single LLM call), encoding and matching takes 0.12s, and refinement averages 4.2s (1.6 rounds before early stopping). Total online latency is 6.1s per query over 386 clips. ReasonT2V requires 8.4s due to two-encoder matching and multi-step LLM reasoning with just-in-time specialist invocations. Embedding methods are faster (<0.1s) but achieve below 16% R@1.We will add a runtime table in the revision. 4.Implementation Details and Reproducibility (R2, Meta): We will release full prompt templates, decoding configurations (temperature=0.3, top-p=0.95 for imagination; temperature=0.1 for refinement), and metadata specifications in the supplementary. The anonymized code repository (noted by R1, R3) contains all prompts and reproducible training scripts. We will also document generation robustness: across 5 runs, the LLM produces valid ActDT JSON in 97.4% of imagination calls, with malformed outputs caught by schema validation and re-prompted automatically. 5.Performance vs. Benchmark-Specific Patterns (R1): Three observations argue against benchmark overfitting. First, the scalability analysis shows R@1 remains stable (57.6% to 55.8%) when expanding the candidate pool from 96 to 386 clips with held-out recordings, indicating no corpus-specific shortcuts. Second, all results are averaged over five seeds with reported standard deviations. Third, the cross-procedure transfer result (Point 1) confirms OR3 maintains its advantage on unseen procedures.

title: Research Design Considerations for Empirical User Studies in MICCAI
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper offers an exceptionally clear and detailed translation of the four validities (internal, external, construct, and statistical conclusion) into the medical context, which is often neglected in algorithm-focused papers. 2.It provides a comprehensive playbook for researchers, covering critical design elements such as variable control, participant selection, and bias mitigation. This is highly valuable for bridging the gap between benchtop engineering and bedside validation. 3.As the community moves toward human-centered AI and AR systems, this paper sets a standard for how these systems should be evaluated, potentially reducing the prevalence of poorly designed pilot studies.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.While the theoretical framework is sound, the paper lacks a concrete worked example or a case study demonstrating how these guidelines can be applied to a specific MICCAI problem (e. g. , evaluating an AI-based diagnostic tool). 2.Additionally, the significant conceptual overlap with another submission is problematic. It appears the authors have split a single contribution into two manuscripts.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

It clearly identifies gaps in current practices and provides practical, well-structured guidance for designing controlled user studies. The discussion is comprehensive, covering multiple stages of study design from planning to execution, and effectively bridges concepts from human-computer interaction and medical imaging. Another strength is the emphasis on reproducibility, transparency, and real-world clinical relevance, which enhances the paper’s impact and applicability. The inclusion of practical considerations and real challenges, such as recruitment and measurement validity, makes the work valuable for researchers planning empirical studies.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper is largely conceptual and does not introduce a novel technical method or empirical validation, which may limit its perceived contribution compared to more technical submissions. While it provides useful guidelines, many of the discussed principles are adapted from established literature in human-computer interaction and psychology, and the paper could better highlight what is uniquely tailored to MICCAI. reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Clinical Relevance: The paper addresses a highly relevant topic, since human-centered development is essential for successfully translating research into clinical practice. This mirrors the cited recent evolution in Explainable AI (XAI), where the integration of HCI principles is becoming indispensable for making model explanations truly actionable in medical settings. Critical Methodological Reflection: The work provides a critique of current practices, such as the reliance on crowdsourcing platforms like Prolific for user recruitment. It correctly highlights the potential gap between high-quality data collection in controlled environments and the actual ecological validity required for real-world clinical applications. Transparency and Reproducibility: The paper promotes a culture where limitations are clearly recognized and research can be more reliably reproduced. The call for greater transparency in reporting human-based evaluations is a significant strength. The community is currently open to sharing code and should likewise commit to sharing the specific details of the conditions for each human evaluation. This will allow us to recognize its limitations. reviewer_3_weaknesses: Abstraction: While the proposed considerations are conceptually sound, they occasionally remain at a high level of abstraction. The practical utility of the work would be significantly enhanced if the authors provided a more concrete “action plan” or a case study demonstrating how to operationalize these qualitative guidelines within a specific MICCAI-related technical project. -Trade-offs: The paper advocates for HCI practices without a sufficient discussion on the subsequent costs and trade-offs. For instance, while pilot studies are essential for identifying protocol flaws and technical bugs, they extend research timelines and resource requirements. A discussion on how to balance these gold-standard principles with the practical constraints of typical research cycles would be beneficial. reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged by the recognition of our work’s importance in MICCAI, including its relevance to human-centered evaluations and their impact (R1, R2), the five key aspects highlighted (R1, R2, R4), and its clinical relevance (R1, R4). Below, we grouped main concerns identified both in the meta-review and in the reviewer’s comments, and we responded to how these will be addressed in the camera-ready version. <Abstract and conceptual framework (R1, R2, R4)> We agree that demonstrating the framework’s practical utility would strengthen its value and better ground the proposed considerations for conducting empirical user studies. Therefore, we will present a case study based on a MICCAI publication from previous years. Through this example, we will illustrate how the considerations apply to methodologies previously used to design and evaluate medical systems with human involvement. For example, consider publication “You, F., Khakhar, R., Picht, T., & Dobbelstein, D. (2020). VR simulation of novel hands-free interaction concepts for surgical robotic visualization systems. In International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (pp. 440-450)”. <Novelty and contribution (R2)> We believe the value of our paper lies in its potential impact on improving research quality and clinical translation in MIC and CAI. The principles are intentionally adapted from established HCI and psychology literature, and this grounding is precisely what makes them reliable and actionable. However, these principles require tailoring to MICCAI’s unique constraints: specialized clinical populations, safety-critical applications, physical system interactions (surgical navigation, robotics, phantoms), and domain-specific measurement challenges. We will clarify these MICCAI-specific adaptations more explicitly in the manuscript. <Discussion of practical considerations (R4)> We will add discussion acknowledging that pilot studies extend timelines, clinician recruitment involves significant logistical challenges, and high-fidelity simulations require substantial investment. We will address how researchers can prioritize considerations given practical constraints. < Overlap with another submission (R1)> The related survey paper was not accepted at the main conference. This submission is self-contained and stands independently, providing methodology considerations for controlled user studies. We will remove references to the companion paper. We will remove subsection numbers from Figure 1 (R4) and simplify dense sections for improved readability (R2), such as the Technology System Design and User Task and Interfaces sections. By simplifying these sections, we create space to include suggestions raised in previous points.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a structured framework for designing empirical user studies in medical image computing and computer-assisted interventions, adapting established HCI concepts to promote more rigorous and clinically relevant evaluations. All reviewers provided consistent positive evaluations (score = 4), highlighting the importance and timeliness of the topic, as well as the clarity and potential impact of the work on improving research practices within the MICCAI community. The main limitations noted by the reviewers are that the contribution is largely conceptual, lacks a concrete case study or illustrative example, and has limited novelty due to reliance on existing HCI principles. Another issue is that the discussion of practical trade-offs and feasibility could be further strengthened, and a potential overlap with another submission should be clarified. Despite these limitations, no major methodological flaws were identified, and the weaknesses primarily relate to presentation and completeness rather than fundamental issues. Based on the consistent positive evaluations and the relevance of the contribution, a provisional accept is recommended. The authors are encouraged to include a concrete example, clarify novelty, discuss practical considerations, and address the potential overlap in the final version.

title: REVEAL++: Differentiable Phenotypic Grouping for Vision–Language Retinal Modeling of Alzheimer’s Disease Risk
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The proposed method extends the REVEAL with a soft Phenotypic Grouping within contrastive learning and shows an advantage in AD risk prediction
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Clarity of the overall framework: The overall framework is not clearly presented. The proposed method appears to be built upon REVEAL, but this prior work is not properly cited in the main text. Although the REVEAL paper is included in the reference list, it is not explicitly referenced where relevant, which affects clarity and attribution. 2.Task definition: The task is not clearly defined. In particular, it is unclear what form the Alzheimer’s disease (AD) risk prediction takes (e. g. , classification, regression, or risk score estimation). 3.Clarity of notation: The definition of symbols needs to be clarified. For example, the meaning of \tau in Section 2.3 is not clearly explained, which may lead to confusion.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) The paper presents a clear and well-motivated improvement over the prior method, where the hard threshold-based phenotypic grouping strategy in REVEAL is effectively redesigned into continuous phenotypic weighting considering the limitations of introducing hard artificial boundaries, resulting in improved performance. (2) The proposed modifications are clearly described, and implementation details and hyperparameter settings are sufficiently documented, facilitating reproducibility. (3) The experimental results show consistent performance gains over a range of visual-language baselines and the prior method REVEAL, indicating that the proposed modifications are practically effective.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) The overall methodological novelty is somewhat limited, as the proposed method (REVEAL++) is only an modification of the prior work (REVEAL), with relatively minor changes to the original design. (2) The paper only reports performance of the modified model compared to the prior work with a single additional result without more comprehensive analysis. The lack of deeper experimental studies, for example, including comparisons with image-based CNN/Transformer baselines or studies on the contribution of each modality, may limit the overall novelty and the strength of the empirical evidence supporting the proposed improvement.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper presents a clear and conceptually sound methodological contribution. The proposed approach is well motivated and addresses a genuine limitation of the GACL approach. The formulation is elegant, integrates naturally into standard contrastive objectives, and appears novel in this context. The paper is nicely structured and the methodology is easy to follow, supported by a strong visual overview in Fig. 1.The combination of intra-modality similarity to define phenotypic relationships and cross-modality similarity for alignment is well thought through. The experimental evaluation is thorough and convincing. The use of a large-scale dataset (UK Biobank) strengthens the empirical claims, and the inclusion of strong baselines, including prior work from the same line of research, provides a fair comparison. Running experiments across multiple random seeds further supports the robustness of the results. Empirically, the method consistently outperforms baselines and improves upon the prior REVEAL framework, suggesting that the proposed weighting mechanism provides meaningful gains. Finally, the paper is generally well written and clearly structured, with only minor issues in notation and clarity.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The most significant issue is the lack of detail regarding the AD prediction task itself. Key information such as disease prevalence, label definition, and task setup is missing from the main paper. While these details are available in the supplementary material (as prior work), they should be briefly summarised in the main manuscript to ensure the results are interpretable and self-contained. There are also some minor clarity issues in the methodology. The distinction between encoders and projection layers is not fully clear, and the notation appears slightly inconsistent across sections. Specifically, Section 2.3 should be clarified: $E_I$ and $E_T$ are described as encoders, and the projection layers described as separate components. However, it would seem from the rest of the description that $E_I$ and $E_T$ include the projection layers. Please make this explicit, confirming that $\mathbf{z}^{I} p \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\mathbf{z}^{T}_p \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$, if that’s indeed the case. There’s also no need to redefine $\hat{\mathbf{z}} {p}^{I}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{p}^{T}$ in Section 2.4, as they’re already introduced in Section 2.3.Additionally, Section 3.2 discusses how the phenotypic similarity thresholds were selected, but the details are quite vague. Please also be clear that this refers to $\tau_F$ and $\tau_T$ from Section 2.4 / Equation 4, if indeed it does. Another key concern is reproducibility. The paper does not provide an anonymised code repository or a commitment to release it upon acceptance, which limits transparency and the ability to verify results. More broadly, while the method achieves state-of-the-art performance, the absolute performance remains modest (AUC ~0.68), and the paper does not sufficiently contextualise this in terms of task difficulty or clinical relevance.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that reviewers recognized REVEAL++ as a “clear and well-motivated improvement” (R2), a “conceptually sound methodological contribution” with an “elegant” formulation (R3), and a method that addresses a genuine limitation of hard GACL by replacing discrete grouping with continuous phenotypic weighting (R2, R3, Meta). We also appreciate that reviewers found the results consistently improved over REVEAL and other vision-language baselines (R2, R3, Meta). Q1: (R1, R3, Meta) What exactly is the AD risk prediction task? A1: The submitted experiments formulate incident AD prediction as a binary classification task. Participants free of AD at baseline retinal imaging are labeled positive if they subsequently develop AD during follow-up, while controls do not meet the AD definition during follow-up. Evaluation is performed using subject-level splits and classification metrics: AUROC, balanced accuracy, F1, and MCC. We will revise Sec. 3.1/Table 1 to include label construction, case/control counts, prevalence, split structure, and evaluation protocol. Q2: (R1, R2, Meta) What is inherited from REVEAL, and what is new? A2: REVEAL++ is intentionally built on REVEAL. The inherited components are the retinal image-clinical narrative alignment setting, RETFound/GatorTron encoders, and the motivation for group-aware contrastive learning. The new contribution is replacing REVEAL’s binary thresholded group membership with a differentiable phenotypic weighting matrix and a soft-target multi-positive contrastive objective. This changes the supervision from hard positive/negative assignment to graded pairwise phenotypic similarity, which better matches the continuum-like nature of preclinical AD progression. We will explicitly cite REVEAL where inherited components are introduced and distinguish between inherited and new components in Sec. 2.Q3: (R1, R3, Meta) Can the notation be clarified? A3: In the submitted method, image/text backbones and projection heads are separate components. We will revise the notation so E_I and E_T denote the image and text backbone encoders, while P_I and P_T denote the projection heads. We will remove redundant definitions of normalized embeddings. To avoid overloading tau, we will denote contrastive temperature as T_c = exp(-s), reserving tau_F and tau_T for the phenotypic similarity thresholds in Eq. 4.We will also clarify that tau_F and tau_T are tuned as hyperparameters using Optuna over ranges initialized from empirical intra-modality cosine similarity distributions. Q4: (R2, Meta) Are there sufficient ablations and baselines? A4: We appreciate the request for deeper ablations and modality analysis. Since MICCAI rebuttal guidelines do not allow new experimental results in the rebuttal, we cannot introduce additional ablation results here. We clarify that the submitted Table 2 already includes a component comparison between “Ours (no GACL),” “Ours (with GACL),” and “Ours (Phenotypic Weighted),” directly isolating the effect of replacing hard grouping with continuous weighting. This table also compares against retinal and biomedical vision-language baselines, including RETFound+GatorTron, RETCLIP, BiomedCLIP, PMC-CLIP, and KeepFIT-CFP. Q5: (R3, Meta) How should the modest AUROC be interpreted clinically? A5: Our claim is not that an AUROC of around 0.68 is sufficient for standalone clinical deployment. Rather, the results show improved representation learning for a difficult, low-prevalence, long-horizon incident AD prediction task (mean time to diagnosis: 8.68 years) using scalable retinal and clinical risk-factor data. Q6: (R3) How will reproducibility be addressed? A6: We will release an anonymized code repository upon acceptance. UK Biobank raw data cannot be redistributed due to data-use restrictions, but we will provide documentation enabling authorized UK Biobank users to reproduce the submitted experiments.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a soft differentiable phenotypic grouping strategy for vision-language AD risk prediction. Replacing hard phenotype grouping in REVEAL with continuous phenotypic weighting is a well-motivated and elegant idea, and the reported results show consistent gains over REVEAL and other vision-language baselines. However, the novelty is still incremental because the method is mainly an extension of the prior REVEAL framework. The task definition and experimental setup need clearer presentation. The paper should explicitly state what “AD risk prediction” means, including the label definition, disease prevalence, and whether the task is classification, regression, or risk score estimation. Some notation and methodological details, such as the role of thresholds and projection layers, also need clarification. The empirical results are promising, but additional analysis would strengthen the claim. The authors should provide deeper ablations, comparisons with image-only CNN/Transformer baselines, modality contribution analysis, and clearer discussion of the modest absolute AUC and clinical relevance. | The rebuttal satisfactorily clarifies the task definition, the distinction between inherited REVEAL components and the new differentiable phenotypic weighting, notation, threshold selection, clinical interpretation of the modest AUROC, and reproducibility plans. Despite incremental novelty, the consistent empirical gains and positive post-rebuttal consensus support acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The paper proposes REVEAL++, a differentiable phenotypic grouping strategy for vision-language retinal modeling of AD risk. The main contribution is to replace hard threshold-based grouping in REVEAL with continuous phenotypic weighting and a soft-target multi-positive contrastive objective. Although this is an incremental extension of prior REVEAL work, the idea is well motivated, technically clean, and empirically shows consistent gains over REVEAL and other vision-language baselines. The rebuttal addresses several important concerns. The authors clarified that the task is binary incident AD prediction, explained what is inherited from REVEAL versus what is newly introduced, clarified notation and threshold definitions, and appropriately contextualized the modest AUROC as representation learning for a difficult long-horizon risk prediction task rather than standalone clinical deployment. Some limitations remain, including limited novelty, modest absolute performance, and the need for clearer task details and code release in the final version. However, the overall methodological contribution and post-rebuttal reviewer support justify acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After considering the reviews and the rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The paper presents REVEAL++ for retinal image-based AD risk prediction, with a differentiable phenotypic weighting mechanism to better model continuous preclinical AD progression. The rebuttal addressed the main concerns raised during review. The paper shows consistent improvements over REVEAL and several vision-language baselines, and the authors clarified the task definition, notation, evaluation protocol, and new contributions. I therefore recommend acceptance.

title: ROTE: Routing–Timescale Framework for Balanced Expert Allocation in MoE-Based Continual Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Novel Formulation for Routing: Integrating KAN into the MoE gating mechanism is an elegant solution. By leveraging the local plasticity of KAN’s spline functions, the gradient updates are structurally constrained, which effectively prevents the rapid routing collapse seen in standard MLP-based gating. This ensures long-term expert utilization. Clever Timescale Decoupling: The HTL strategy provides a highly logical stability-plasticity balance. By treating the gating network as a “slow” variable and the experts as “fast” variables, the framework maintains global routing consistency while allowing rapid adaptation to new clinical modalities. Strong and Comprehensive Evaluation: The framework is rigorously evaluated across 10 diverse public medical imaging datasets encompassing various modalities (e. g. , CT, MRI, endoscopy, fundus). The method achieves state-of-the-art Incremental Learning DSC (91.52) and Backward Transfer scores (97.70), validating its robustness against severe distribution shifts.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Ambiguity in Prompt Mechanism during Continual Setup: Since the framework builds upon the interactive Segment Anything Model, the distribution and generation strategy of prompts (points/boxes) can vary significantly across different tasks and modalities. The submission does not detail how prompts were provided during the sequential task stream and whether prompt domain gaps affected the continual learning performance. Limited Baselines for MoE Routing: In Table 1, the MoE baseline is primarily compared against Soft MoE with standard MLP and Attention gating. The evaluation would be stronger if compared with other recent task-routing or expert-balancing techniques specifically designed for continual learning.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: This paper studies continual medical image segmentation in a frozen-SAM setting and proposes a routing-timescale framework to address expert allocation imbalance and forgetting in decoder-side soft MoE adaptation. 1.Meaningful and well-motivated problem formulation It addresses a meaningful and realistic problem setting, namely continual medical image segmentation under a frozen SAM backbone and a no-replay constraint, which is well motivated for privacy-constrained clinical deployment. Rather than making a generic continual learning claim, the paper focuses on a concrete bottleneck in decoder-side soft MoE adaptation, namely expert allocation imbalance over long task sequences. 2.Conceptually clean methodological decomposition The proposed framework is conceptually clean: LRSR is introduced to address routing imbalance through KAN-based soft routing, while HTL is designed to stabilize long-term learning via timescale-separated updates of routing and expert parameters. The decomposition of the problem into routing behavior and update dynamics is intuitive and easy to follow. 3.Targeted use of KAN in the routing pathway The paper does not use KAN as a generic replacement block, but instead motivates it through the specific routing problem in MoE-based continual segmentation. The argument that local plasticity may help reduce premature expert monopolization is interesting, and the routing-focused use of KAN is more targeted than a purely capacity-driven architectural substitution. 4.Empirical setup aligned with the stated objective The evaluation is conducted in a continual learning setting over 10 medical image segmentation datasets spanning multiple modalities, and the paper reports not only segmentation performance but also continual-learning-oriented metrics such as IL-DSC and BWT, which are appropriate for assessing long-horizon knowledge retention. 5.The full framework appears empirically effective The reported results show that the full ROTE framework improves over several continual learning baselines and over a standard soft MoE baseline. The ablation analyses provide at least some empirical support that the proposed design is not arbitrary. In addition, the routing and update analyses in Fig. 3 offer qualitative evidence consistent with the intended behavior of the method.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The mechanism-level claims are stronger than the current evidence. In Secs. 2.2–2.3, the paper attributes the benefit of LRSR to KAN-induced local plasticity and the benefit of HTL to timescale-separated routing/expert updates. However, the empirical support is relatively limited. Beyond Table 1, the main evidence is the routing-weight visualization and the routing update interval sweep in Fig. 3.These results support that the full framework is effective, but they do not yet fully validate the stronger causal explanation presented in the method section. The MoE comparison is limited for a paper whose main contribution is improved routing. The core technical story is that standard soft MoE routing collapses and that the proposed KAN-based routing addresses this issue. However, the main direct MoE comparison in Table 1 is against a basic “Soft MoE (MLP gating)” baseline. The paper cites broader MoE routing literature in the references, but these stronger routing/balancing alternatives are not included in the main quantitative comparison. Beyond the proposed KAN router and the MLP-gated Soft MoE baseline in Table 1, the paper only provides an additional routing-weight visualization for attention gating in Fig. 3, without a corresponding full performance comparison. This makes it difficult to judge how much of the gain comes from the specific proposed routing design versus from improving over a relatively simple baseline. 2.The ablation suggests useful synergy, but weakens the modular interpretation. Table 1 shows that LRSR alone changes IL-DSC/BWT only marginally and HTL alone also brings only modest gains, while the substantial improvement appears mainly when both are combined in ROTE. This supports the effectiveness of the combined framework, but it less clearly shows that each component independently solves the specific failure mode attributed to it. 3.Efficiency and complexity are not discussed. Sec. 3.1 reports optimizer and continual-learning settings, but the paper does not report parameter overhead, computational cost, or runtime implications of the KAN-based routing design. Since the empirical gain over the standard Soft MoE baseline is positive but still moderate in absolute magnitude, this omission makes it harder to assess the practical value of the method. 4.Some implementation details remain under-specified. In Sec. 2.1, the method defines the MoE abstractly with K experts and a routing function, but the expert design inside the decoder-side Soft MoE is not described in much detail. Since the claimed contribution is specifically about routing and update strategy, clearer expert-level implementation details would help reproducibility and make it easier to assess fairness across variants. While the authors state in the abstract that code and models will be publicly available, the current manuscript itself still leaves some key implementation details unclear
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper identifies routing imbalance and catastrophic forgetting as two practical issues in MoE-based continual segmentation and addresses them with two corresponding components, which makes the overall framework easy to understand. 2.The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem in continual medical image segmentation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Table 1 states that ROTE achieves the best IL-DSC and BWT, but CODA-Prompt has a higher BWT (98.71 vs. 97.70). In addition, ROTE reports only +0.91 IL-DSC and +0.60 BWT over Soft-MoE+MLP. 2.MoE-based non-forgetting medical segmentation with SAM has already been explored in SAM-Med3D-MoE [16]. Therefore, the paper should provide a clearer comparison with this line of work, to better justify what is new in the proposed framework and how it advances beyond existing approaches.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

However, there exist a few concerns that need to be clarified: 1) why the KAN only delays early routing collapse but fails to deliver promised balancing strategy? 2) whether the traditional load balancing loss is applicable and how they behave in comparison? 3) why the anti-forgetting effect is not well confirmed in Table 1 where the baseline (finetuning, which is prone to specific expert/modality/region) is only with < 2% performance gap with regard to the proposed method? title: Situational context embedding and knowledge-based grounding for LLMs in surgical training assistance
reviewer_1_strengths: The system architecture looks well designed. They combine simulator-derived situational context, guidance documents, THA textbook knowledge, RAG, deterministic scene grounding outside the LLM, and then a constrained response generation step. This gives the system a more specific and grounded system instead of simply applying an LLM directly to the simulator setting.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The approach has more of a system integration contribution than an algorithmic one. The RAG pipeline, abstention mechanism, and query clarification are all fairly standard components. Because of that, the novelty is limited. There are some concerns about the evaluation. The study mainly evaluates question-answer quality rather than actual tutoring effectiveness. So while their method may outperform the baseline model in answer quality, that does not necessarily show that it improves surgical training outcomes. The baseline comparison is somewhat weak. Their baseline is GPT-4.1 with only a brief role instruction, while their full system includes structured simulator state, query clarification, curated simulator documents, textbook knowledge, and abstention. That makes the comparison feel uneven. It would be helpful to include stronger ablation or baseline experiments to show which components contribute most to the performance gains. The current ablation study is also limited, since it uses ROUGE-1 and SBERT similarity to expert reference text rather than expert ratings. One result that stood out was that removing Tier 3 leads to ROUGE-1 = 0.000 and SBERT = -0.005.I am not sure whether that reflects a true collapse of the system or an issue with how abstentions are being handled in the evaluation, but it definitely seems worth questioning. The dataset is also relatively small, which further limits the strength of the conclusions.

reviewer_2_strengths: build a visual question and answer dataset with 60 THA-related questions in pre-operative, process-related, and situational categories. propose LLM-RAG by storing and retrieving situational context and textbook knowledge conduct human evaluation and comparison
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The dataset of 60 questions can be limited. It is unclear how the RAG has been built and retrieval results have been systematically evaluated. reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Dear (meta-)reviewers, Thank you for your positive (R1, R3) and constructive (R2) feedback and the opportunity to revise our work. Novelty (R1, R2): As an application study per the MICCAI Reviewer Guidelines, novelty also lies in clinically relevant system co-design rather than new algorithmic primitives. Our contribution is the joint design of deterministic situational grounding, hierarchical RAG, calibrated abstention, and query clarification, whose interactions and safety properties cannot be investigated in isolation. This will provide a reusable blueprint for building clinically safe LLM-based systems. On R2’s point that calibrated abstention is not sufficiently detailed, it triggers when retrieval confidence falls below an empirically determined L2-distance threshold, producing an explicit non-answer rather than ungrounded text. We will add a more detailed technical explanation to the paper. Evaluation (R1, R3): The absence of learning-outcomes evaluation was a deliberate scoping decision: detecting training impact requires a controlled longitudinal trial with a substantially larger trainee cohort and careful control of confounders. System-level validation, asking whether the pipeline produces accurate, safe, and clinically appropriate responses, is the necessary precursor. We acknowledge that the paper should not claim proven training effectiveness; our results indicate that carefully designed grounding produces clinically appropriate responses. We will ensure the revised manuscript does not overclaim proven training effectiveness beyond what the current evaluation supports. Baseline and ablation (R1, R2): The baseline reflects the most common real-world alternative, namely clinicians and trainees interacting with general-purpose LLMs via brief role prompts. As many published clinical LLM studies consider only general-purpose LLMs as their primary evaluation, quantifying the deficits of this prevalent informal practice in a safety-critical setting is itself a meaningful contribution. Our ablation (Table 2) reports the baseline LLM alongside leave-one-component-out variants (directly addressing R2’s LLM versus LLM-RAG concern), and we will add more detail to the discussion. Removing Tier 3 leads to frequent abstentions by design, producing the ROUGE-1=0 and SBERT≈0 values flagged by R1; we will clarify this in the Results to prevent it from being misread as a system collapse rather than the intended safety mechanism. Dataset size (R1, R2, R3): The involved senior expert surgeons confirmed that the questionnaire is representative for the constrained simulator workflow. We also want to emphasize that the number of questions was deliberately balanced against the realistic time commitment of full-time practicing surgeons, resulting in an evaluation totaling 900 (!) blinded expert ratings (5 surgeons × 3 systems × 60 questions). Supported by R3, we believe that the presented blinded expert study is a strong and meaningful evaluation. Generalizability (R3): Our core modules, the RAG pipeline, abstention mechanism, and query clarification, are procedure-agnostic by design. Adapting to a new procedure or simulator requires swapping the curated knowledge base and redefining the simulator-state representation, which are primarily engineering tasks. Generalizability is therefore a concrete hypothesis for follow-up work and we will include a detailed statement in the discussion section. Reproducibility (R1, R2, R3): We will publish the full code, question catalog, and expert reference answers. We agree that the proprietary-API dependency is a limitation (R1, R3), but want to clarify that it affects only the underlying LLM. Since the architecture is LLM-agnostic by design, substitution with an open-source model should be subject to future work. Ethics (R2, R3): The system was evaluated in a simulator-based educational setting, was not used for patient care or clinical decision-making, and did not involve patient-identifiable data.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): There is a variance of reviews for this paper and should go forward for rebuttal. | The authors are quite honest and aware of the limitations of the study which does provide a strong case for LLM-based surgical tutoring. Indeed, it does seem to provide evidence for Expert-based tutoring, but that is the state of the art. There are concerns for reproducibility. In fact, the result seem to be subjective – and the variance across the results is very low across conditions. This implicates a recommendation for rejection from conference paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After the rebuttal, the majority of reviewers recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal clarifies key points: it better positions the work as an application/system contribution (not algorithmic novelty), explains the abstention mechanism, and explicitly acknowledges that training effectiveness is not evaluated, addressing concerns about overclaiming. It also clarifies that ablations include LLM vs RAG variants and explains abnormal results (e.g., ROUGE=0 due to abstention). title: SS-IoSR: Self-supervised Intraoral Scans Repair
reviewer_1_strengths: The main contribution of this work lies in demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework for intraoral 3D scans.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper has the following limitations: The overall level of novelty is limited. The adopted framework has already been applied in self-supervised point cloud completion for general scenarios, and the authors do not provide sufficient task-specific improvements, making the novelty unclear. There are several unclear aspects in the method description. For example, in the first stage, it is not specified whether the masked point cloud is fed into the MAE as a whole or processed patch-by-patch. The concept of the masked token in Figure 1 is not clearly explained. Additionally, when the input point cloud contains missing regions, it is unclear how the seed points are selected. author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and are encouraged that R3 recognizes the clinical relevance and effectiveness of our results. This rebuttal addresses concerns regarding novelty, methodology, and reproducibility. #Novelty & IoSR Comparison (R1, R2): SS-IoSR introduces a novel Self-Supervised paradigm for intraoral scan repair, addressing fundamental limitations in existing literature: Data & Learning Novelty: Unlike supervised frameworks relying on paired “clean/defective” scans, our Phase 1 Masked Autoencoder (MAE) learns the dental geometry manifold directly from raw, unlabeled clinical data. Unlike MAE frameworks for general 3D shapes, our method is specifically adapted to intraoral scans, where highly non-uniform densities and complex structures make standard KNN-based patching unreliable. We introduce a density-aware fixed-radius patch strategy to preserve anatomical coherence across irregular surfaces. This eliminates synthetic defect bias and demonstrates that self-supervised priors, when tailored to dental topology, outperform supervised synthetic training. Conceptual & Architectural Shift: While IoSR uses a global strategy, SS-IoSR focuses on localized repair to preserve high-frequency details (e.g., incisal edges) that global methods oversmooth. We leverage a Transformer-based MAE for long-range geometric reasoning across patches. Crucially, our ablation studies show that self-supervised methods without implicit geometric modeling are insufficient; thus, we introduce a DPSR-based implicit refinement block (IRB) to recover fine-grained inter-dental details and maintain surface continuity, ensuring clinical fidelity where explicit reconstructions fail. #Methodological Details (R1, R3): Patch-wise Processing: In Stage 1, the point cloud is processed patch-by-patch. We utilize a fixed-radius strategy (3mm) rather than KNN to ensure a consistent geometric scale, critical for dental scans where point density varies significantly based on scanner hardware. Masked Tokens: Masked tokens are learnable geometric placeholders. Combined with positional embeddings, they serve as spatial queries that allow the decoder to identify the locations of missing regions and reconstruct their coordinates based on the surrounding anatomical context. Seed Point Selection: Seed points are clinician-selected to indicate the centroid of a defect (e.g., the centroid of a hole’s boundary polyline). This human-in-the-loop (HITL) paradigm is the most effective strategy for clinical safety; it ensures repairs are targeted and avoids “hallucinations” common in fully autonomous models. This is vital as real-world defects are typically limited in scale; repairing massive gaps is often unnecessary and lacks patient-specific anatomical reference. Our sensitivity analysis confirms robustness to selection variability up to 1mm. #Literature & Implicit Models (R2): We thank R2 for the citations (e.g., NPHM, Zhang et al.), which we will include. Unlike DeepSDF, our implicit module performs per-case optimization to preserve clinical fidelity rather than global class-based modeling. Unlike Zhang et al., which requires explicit tooth-level identification and occupancy vectors, SS-IoSR operates on raw, arbitrary surfaces, bypassing the need for prior segmentation or tooth-level labeling. #Sensitivity, Limitations, & Reproducibility (R1, R2, R3): The 3mm radius was defined with dental experts to balance context and precision. We will add a dedicated section on limitations: SS-IoSR may struggle with extensive structural loss (e.g., missing an entire crown) where local context is insufficient. Future work could integrate global shape priors as a guide. Finally, we officially commit to releasing the source code, models, and our paired dataset upon acceptance. This will establish the first standardized benchmark for dental scan restoration. A professional linguistic revision (R1) will be performed to clarify Stage 1/2 transitions.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that they identified several strengths: the paper addresses a timely problem for MICCAI, opens discussion on the sustainability and quality of peer review, and proposes a practical reproducibility-screening framework. Reviewers appreciated that Paper-Snitch is not an automated reviewer, but an auxiliary tool for verifiability. They also highlighted evidence-grounded design, static inspection without executing untrusted code, interpretable analyses, deterministic scoring, actionable recommendations, human agreement, and available code/demo resources. Scope and role in peer review. Paper-Snitch is intended only to support reviewers or chairs with auditable checks of objective artifact signals; final judgment remains human. We will strengthen this framing. Privacy. Submissions cannot be sent to external AI services without policy, consent, and processing guarantees. The current implementation is a proof-of-concept; the framework is model-agnostic. There are multiple options to evaluate when moving to production: running the pipeline in a controlled environment, disabling external web search during double-blind review, using local/open-weight models, storing minimal audit artifacts, or ensuring that manuscripts and repositories are not used for model training with a specific contract signed with service providers. Regarding bias, prompt injection, and robustness , LLM-assisted peer review can introduce risks. Paper-Snitch mitigates some of them by restricting LLMs to evidence retrieval and structured criterion assessment, while scores are computed deterministically. This does not eliminate bias, but provides tools for mitigation. Like medical imaging tools that assist expert clinicians and surgeons in daily clinical workflows—supporting, standardizing, and accelerating specific tasks without replacing professional judgment—Paper-Snitch is designed to play an analogous role in the peer-review process. It provides reviewers and chairs with structured, evidence-grounded reproducibility checks, helping them identify missing or unverifiable artifacts more consistently while leaving all scientific and acceptance decisions to human experts. For prompt injection, schema-constrained outputs and deterministic tree checks are used. We avoid executing untrusted code. Evaluation. 100 MICCAI 2025 papers are an initial validation rather than definitive evidence of generalizability. We will clarify that the papers were randomly sampled and stratified by method, dataset, and both. Model choice and baselines. Both GPT-4o and GPT-5 were evaluated under the same embeddings and scoring code. Notably, the demo is designed with extensibility in mind, and models powering the tool can be configured at runtime. Future extensions will include a thorough evaluation of open-source and local alternatives, including Ollama-served models, alongside agentic tools such as Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and OpenAI Codex. Regarding code-analysis fragility, non-standard repositories may challenge file selection. We will clarify this limitation and note that repository templates or required entry points would improve reliability. Jupyter notebooks are handled statically as JSON/text artifacts: markdown, imports, cells, commands, and outputs can be inspected, but notebooks are not executed. Finally, we clarify the provenance of Fig. 1. The MICCAI code-availability statistics are part of this study and are produced by the code-availability node applied to the analyzed MICCAI corpus.

title: Tooth Alignment via Virtual Trajectories with Clinical Constraints
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper presents a well-designed approach to tooth alignment, with several strengths: First, the formulation of tooth alignment as a multi-step trajectory prediction problem is an intuitive departure from standard one-shot regression approaches. By decomposing large transformations into incremental steps, the method reflects the underlying structure of the problem and leads to improved performance. Second, the work stands out in its use of domain-informed modeling. In particular, the incorporation of clinically motivated constraints at intermediate stages is a well-motivated design choice that aligns the optimization process with the clinical properties of tooth movement. This is further strengthened by the training strategy, including trajectory stabilization and intermediate-state self-learning. Together, these components form a coherent framework where both the objective and training are tailored to the problem. Finally, the method shows consistent quantitative improvements over compared baselines across multiple metrics. Overall, the paper combines a solid methodological design, and a convincing empirical performance.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: First, some of the claims are overstated. In particular, the paper claims to “mimic the stage-wise decision-making process” of clinical orthodontic treatment. However, the proposed method does not model decision-making in a meaningful sense: it does not include any mechanism for action selection, adapting decisions based on intermediate outcomes, or explicitly representing clinical reasoning. Instead, it enforces predefined constraints during optimization. While this introduces a process-like structure, it should not be equated with mimicking clinical decision-making, and the claim should be toned down. Second, several component-level interpretations are insufficiently supported by the presented experiments. For example, the paper attributes roles to individual components, such as TSS “stabilizing early trajectory learning” or self-learning “densifying trajectories. ” However, the experimental results (e. g. , ablation study) mainly demonstrate improvements in final performance metrics, without directly validating these more detailed behavioral claims. As a result, some of these statements read as the authors’ interpretations rather than empirically established effects. Third, some design choices are introduced without sufficient motivation. For instance, the number of trajectory steps (K=21) is a central parameter but is not justified. Similarly, the decision to apply trajectory stabilization only during early training is not explained. Providing intuition or empirical justification for these aspects would improve clarity.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: This paper presents a process-centric framework for automatic tooth alignment, replacing one-shot endpoint regression with staged SE(3) refinement under intermediate clinical constraints. The idea is interesting and well motivated, and the proposed approach achieves competitive performance compared with the reported baselines. The ablation study is also informative and suggests that a substantial portion of the performance improvement arises from the progressive modeling strategy.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: My main concern is that the learned “trajectory” remains a virtual trajectory derived from pre-/post-treatment pairs, rather than a clinically validated treatment trajectory. The intermediate supervision is constructed through geodesic pseudo-targets, stage-wise constraints, and self-learning signals. As a result, while the paper demonstrates improved staged refinement behavior, it does not yet clearly establish that the model captures real clinical treatment dynamics. The corresponding claims should therefore be moderated to better reflect this limitation. A second concern relates to the experimental comparison. The current evaluation is still largely dominated by one-shot regression baselines. While this setup supports the argument that progressive modeling can outperform one-shot prediction, it does not fully demonstrate competitiveness with more recent trajectory-oriented or diffusion-based approaches. In addition, the proposed trajectory stabilization strategy relies on several strong priors, such as relatively uniform per-stage movements and geodesic pseudo-targets, whose clinical realism and practical justification are not yet fully discussed.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Novel Progressive Trajectory Modeling Paradigm. Existing methods mostly regress the final transformation directly, ignoring the clinical importance of intermediate stages. This paper is the first to formulate tooth alignment as a multi-step SE(3) trajectory and achieve progressive movement through cumulative composition. This paradigm is pioneering in automated orthodontic planning. 2.Clever Design of Trajectory Stabilization Strategy. Training a multi-step trajectory using only pre-treatment and post-treatment data can easily lead to trajectory collapse, such as excessively large single-step displacements or failure to converge. The proposed TSS addresses this problem through uniform movement regularization, which encourages all teeth to move equally at each step, and geodesic pseudo-target interpolation, which provides soft supervision for intermediate steps. Moreover, TSS is applied only in the early training phase using a cosine schedule, so it does not interfere with later fine learning. 3.Use of Only Pre-treatment and Post-treatment Data. Many clinical datasets contain only the initial and final scans without intermediate stage annotations. The proposed method does not rely on intermediate labels, which gives it high practicality and strong generalization potential.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1: Lack of validation against real clinical intermediate states. The paper does not use any real patient intermediate scans to verify whether the generated virtual trajectories match actual tooth movement. It is recommended to include even a small amount of real intermediate data for qualitative comparison or cite existing biomechanical studies. 2.The choice of K=21 lacks justification. The paper fixes K=21 without providing clinical or experimental grounds for this value. .

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. We appreciate that the clinical relevance of process-centric tooth alignment and progressive virtual trajectories with stage-wise constraints were recognized. [On clinical decision-making — R1, R2] We agree that “mimicking stage-wise clinical decision-making” should be interpreted carefully. Our method does not model full clinical reasoning, action selection, or clinician-specific policies. Rather, it approximates a process-centric alignment workflow by evaluating collision avoidance, occlusal-plane consistency, and spacing control at each virtual stage, not only at the final configuration. We will moderate this wording with expressions such as “process-centric alignment with stage-wise evaluation” and “virtual progressive tooth movement trajectory with intermediate-stage clinical constraints,” and clarify that such claims indicate a long-term direction, not a fully realized capability. [On virtual trajectories — R2, R3] We acknowledge that generated trajectories are learned from pre-/post-treatment pairs, not clinically observed intermediate trajectories. As noted in the Introduction, most public/real-world datasets provide only pre-/post-treatment pairs; thus, our goal is a practical framework under this data constraint, not recovery of true patient-specific biological movement. It decomposes large one-shot transformations into progressive SE(3) updates and enables intermediate constraint enforcement from only pre-/post-treatment data. We will clarify that refined trajectory modeling with intermediate scans/data remains future work. [On dataset/failure cases — Meta-review, R2, R3] We acknowledge that evaluation on diverse malocclusion types, jaw morphologies, and difficult cases would strengthen generalizability. Our evaluation uses the public paired pre-/post-treatment IOS dataset with 5-fold cross-validation and geometric/motion metrics, but intermediate scans and extreme scenarios remain beyond scope. We will state these limitations and discuss the need for further analyses, including severe crowding and anchorage-critical cases. [On K=21 and early TSS — R1, R3] We will better justify K=21.It was selected as a staged refinement length motivated by prior clear-aligner studies reporting sequences around this scale, while keeping rollout tractable. It is not an exact clinical treatment schedule. TSS is mainly applied in early training because geodesic pseudo-targets and movement regularization provide an initial scaffold; later training is driven by final alignment and stage-wise constraints. We will clarify this and cite prior aligner studies. [On component interpretation — R1] Component-level roles should be stated cautiously. The ablation study shows final-performance gains from progressive modeling, stage-wise constraints, TSS, and self-learning, but does not directly prove all behavioral interpretations. We will revise statements such as “TSS stabilizes early trajectory learning” and “self-learning densifies trajectories” to clarify that these are design motivations and interpretations supported by ablation trends and visualization, not established clinical effects. [On comparison scope — R2] Comparisons with recent diffusion-based methods would be valuable references. However, our main contribution is not a stronger architecture, but a paradigm shift from one-shot endpoint prediction to progressive trajectory prediction with stage-wise constraints. We will clarify this scope and discuss model-level extensions without overstating competitiveness. [On presentation/reproducibility — R1, R2] We will improve clarity by unifying notation, correcting grammar/LaTeX issues, clarifying Figs. 1/2, replacing “Scan,” and adding implementation details. We will also release code to support reproducibility. We appreciate the reviewers’ feedback and will improve clarity, positioning, and clinical interpretation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a novel formulation for tooth alignment that plans virtual trajectories under clinically meaningful constraints, most notably the avoidance of inter-tooth collisions during the simulated alignment process. The key contribution is the introduction of a trajectory-based optimization framework that explicitly models the biomechanical and spatial constraints inherent in orthodontic treatment planning, moving beyond static target pose estimation. Reviewer R1 characterized this work as “a standout contribution” with a “clear, well-executed idea that produces strong results on a challenging problem,” while R2 acknowledged the “clinical relevance and the clear improvement over existing methods.” Both reviewers recognized the technical soundness and practical importance of the approach. R1’s score of 5 (Accept) reflects enthusiasm for the novelty and execution, noting that the method addresses a real gap in current computational orthodontics by ensuring that planned tooth movements are physically plausible and collision-free throughout the entire treatment sequence. R2, assigning a score of 4 (Weak Accept), similarly appreciated the clinical framing and the demonstrable performance gains over baseline approaches, which supports the paper’s value to the MICCAI community. The primary limitation, as noted by R2, concerns the evaluation dataset, which was described as “somewhat limited.” While the results are convincing within the presented scope, a larger and more diverse set of clinical cases (e.g., varying degrees of malocclusion, different jaw morphologies) would strengthen the generalizability claims. Additionally, neither reviewer deeply interrogated potential failure cases, such as extreme crowding or anchorage-critical scenarios, which remain open questions for future work. Nonetheless, these limitations do not undermine the core contribution, which is well-supported by the evidence provided. Given the strong average score of 4.5, the clear enthusiasm from R1, and the overall positive assessment from R2 regarding clinical relevance and methodological improvement, there is a clear consensus that this work meets the high bar for acceptance at MICCAI 2026.The novelty of formulating tooth alignment as a trajectory planning problem under clinical constraints is compelling, and the execution demonstrated is rigorous enough to warrant publication. I therefore recommend unconditional acceptance.

title: VisiFAT: Estimating Visceral Fat from Dual-View DXA Scans Using Cross-View Attention
reviewer_1_strengths: The approach, while technically not novel, provides an interesting application of the technique to solve a practical medical problem.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The related work section seems a bit thin. Using cross-view attention with consistency loss is a standard architectural adaptation rather than a major novel approach. In the VAT estimation literature, the comparisons lean heavily on a key prior model. It will be helpful if the table title uses RMSE (g) and MAE (g) with units. Additionally, Table 1 and Table 3 show the proposed model’s sMAPE at 17.85%, but Table 2 cites Cross-view Attn. + CVC regularisation at 17.25%. Are these referring to the same final model? The paper state that the framework captures three-dimensional body composition cues not observable from either view alone. Is there any direct proof? The comparison to Maqsood et al. employs LS with age, weight, and height, while the proposed model uses LS+PAS with sex, age, weight, and height, which isn’t a controlled apples-to-apples comparison. For a better setting, they could also use the same backbone, same optimization recipe, possibly a “proposed architecture with LS only” control.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper presents a detailed model architecture featuring a novel cross-view attention fusion (CVAF) mechanism designed to integrate different modalities effectively. To maintain consistency across perspectives, the authors implement CVC regularization, which ensures that VAT estimations remain stable regardless of the input image view. The experimental section is rigorous, offering extensive benchmark comparisons and ablation studies that clarify the specific contributions of each technical novelty and demonstrate how the approach outperforms conventional multi-view fusion strategies. Most importantly, the authors ground their technical findings in real-world impact by including a clinical validation that correlates their results with diabetes and cardiovascular events.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The authors demonstrate clear improvements with the VisiFAT model compared to single-view and non-attention baselines. To help strengthen the impact of the work, there are a few areas where further clarification would be very beneficial: Regarding the choice of ground truth, could the authors clarify the decision to use CoreScan estimations? Since this study utilizes the UK Biobank, do we have access to MRI data for many participants to see how VisiFAT performs against MRI-derived VAT? This would be particularly helpful, since some studies show that DXA-based estimates, such as CoreScan, can exhibit systematic biases at the extremes of the VAT distribution. There are also a few questions regarding the preprocessing steps that might help readers better understand the methodology. Given the broad size ranges for the LS and PAS views, how was anatomical consistency maintained across scans that may cover different regions of the body? If the views are focused specifically on the spine rather than the whole body, it would be helpful to clarify what features the model is primarily learning from. Additionally, it would be useful to know how the authors maintained a constant physical resolution during the resizing process, and what the reasoning was behind the specific cropping and padding strategy used. In the multivariable-adjusted logistic regression models, what was the motivation for including the scan year as a covariate? Understanding how this variable interacts with the model’s predictions would be very helpful for evaluating its generalizability to other clinical settings. Regarding the validation strategy, while the 80/10/10 split is a rigorous way to use the available data, knowing if the model was tested on a completely isolated dataset would add confidence in its real-world performance.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses an important clinical problem, namely scalable VAT estimation without relying on costly imaging modalities such as MRI or CT. The use of multi-view DXA data is well motivated and represents a meaningful extension beyond existing single-view approaches. The integration of demographic information alongside imaging data is appropriate and practically relevant. The clinical analysis, particularly the association with cardiovascular disease prevalence, is a strong aspect of the work and enhances its translational value. The method shows quantitative improvements over baselines, suggesting the benefit of the proposed multi-view fusion strategy.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Conceptual and Positioning Issues The claim of extracting 3D information from only two DXA views appears somewhat strong and may not be fully justified. This statement should be softened or better supported. The Introduction contains overly strong claims regarding MRI. There are large-scale longitudinal studies that successfully use MRI for SAT and VAT quantification. Moreover, MRI provides additional advantages such as fat fraction estimation, which is not available with CT or DXA. While the argument about cost and efficiency is valid, the current wording should be revised to avoid being misleading. Emphasizing the accessibility and low cost of DXA would be a more balanced positioning. Methodological Clarity The description of the dual-view image encoders is unclear. Specifically, it is not explained where the number “3” comes from (e.g., whether it corresponds to three slices per case). When flattening feature maps into token sequences, it is unclear how spatial information is preserved in the latent representation. The cross-view attention fusion (CVAF) module is insufficiently distinguished from a standard transformer. The current description largely mirrors standard attention mechanisms, making the novelty unclear. The cross-view consistency regularization requires further clarification. The use of a squared distance loss is not well justified; in contrast, contrastive losses may provide a more flexible and softer alignment mechanism. A clear formulation and rationale are needed. Baselines and Experimental Design The multi-view baseline is not described in sufficient detail. More explanation is needed to allow proper comparison with the proposed method. The single-view approach is referenced in the Results but not adequately described in the Methods, making it difficult to interpret the comparison. Paper Organization The Results and Discussion should be a separate section, rather than as a subsection of the Methods.

As a result, the comparison primarily demonstrates the benefit of using a strong, domain-specific pretrained model rather than introducing a fundamentally new reward-learning paradigm. The construction of attribute-specific evaluation subsets using MONET scores (S(x,a) ≥ 0.7) could introduce evaluation bias, as the same model influences both reward and evaluation reference sets. The hyperparameter τ = 0.25 for suppressing attributes in the “none” setting is not convincingly justified. MONET scores are known to be noisier and systematically lower for clinical images compared to dermoscopic images, raising concerns that this threshold may be dataset- or modality-specific rather than generally valid. The sensitivity of results to this threshold is not analysed.
