author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing the clarity and relevance of VL-RewardGen. Novelty & MONET Use (R1-R3) VL-RewardGen is not a new DDPO optimizer, but a label-efficient reward formulation for controllable medical image generation. The key idea is to leverage a specialty-specific vision-language (VL) model to convert continuous image-concept alignment into rewards when fine-grained labels are scarce. Our reward design explicitly separates lesion identity from dermoscopic attributes: MEL/NV are mutually exclusive and use a competition-based lesion reward, whereas attributes may be absent, singly present, or co-expressed. This structural distinction ensures that our framework is not a simple binary classifier replacement. Empirically (Table 1), directly optimizing this continuous VL alignment outperforms both the label-supervised reward baseline and a discrete variant that naively binarizes MONET scores using a 0.5 cutoff. Our ablation supports that generic VL models (CLIP/PMC-CLIP) lack sufficient grounding in fine-grained dermoscopic morphology, justifying specialty-grounded rewards. Evaluation & Thresholds (R1, R2) Dermoscopic attribute labels are notoriously scarce. Regarding R2’s suggestion to evaluate MILK-10K’s 7 descriptors, MILK-10K—from ISIC (the largest skin lesion consortium)—provides MONET-derived scores, not clinician gold standards. While direct comparison is challenging, ISIC’s adoption of MONET for benchmarking validates it as a reliable proxy. We use these scores to construct concept-enriched reference distributions, serving as an evaluation metric without expert labels. Derm7pt is one of few datasets with expert labels, essential for training the RL4Med-DDPO baseline—a high-cost dependency our framework eliminates. Thus, our MONET filtering (S(x,a)>=0.7) serves as a robust proxy for high-confidence concepts. Regarding R1’s concern on MONET’s accuracy, our framework utilizes continuous semantic alignment scores rather than categorical labels. These provide richer guidance than deterministic labels, ensuring robustness to reward noise. Our 0.7 cutoff minimizes false positives while avoiding extreme thresholds (e.g., 0.9) that could bias evaluation. Regarding the none-attribute threshold (tau=0.25) in Eq.2 (R2), it acts as a conservative margin to separate feature presence from absence without harsh zero-score penalties. This tunable hyper-parameter is readily adjustable for other modalities, such as clinical images. Scope, Utility & Extensibility (R1-R3) This work serves as an initial proof-of-concept for specialty-grounded VL rewards. MEL/NV were chosen as central diagnostic categories, and pigment network/blue-white veil as clinically distinct attributes. Our goal is to demonstrate that VL rewards can steer generation without attribute-labeled reward training. While the downstream classification serves as a supporting utility analysis to show that augmented samples preserve core morphology, we agree that deeper statistical validation is important. Extending this framework to broader taxonomies, alongside comprehensive statistical analysis, is a vital future direction. Furthermore, our methodology is inherently adaptable; by integrating other medical domain-specific VL models—such as EyeCLIP (Shi et al., 2025) for computational ophthalmology—VL-RewardGen can be generalized to synthesize rich, highly targeted medical images. Clinical Use & Skin Color (R1, R3) Generated images are not intended to replace patient data, but to act as targeted augmentation for underrepresented concept combinations. Skin color representation is critical for fair dermatology AI. However, skin tone is typically defined through numerical scales (e.g., Fitzpatrick 1-6) rather than the natural-language dermoscopic labels currently handled by MONET. Integrating multimodal numerical skin-tone descriptors into VL rewards is an excellent direction for future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reviewing this manuscript alongside the expert evaluations, I note that the reviewers recognize a clear and relevant problem, a well-written presentation, and a potentially useful use of dermatology-specific vision–language rewards for controllable image generation. At the same time, there are important concerns regarding the limited experimental scope, dependence on MONET, possible reward–evaluation coupling, insufficient justification of thresholds, and limited analysis across broader attributes, lesion types, and skin tones. Given that these issues may be clarified or partially addressed through additional explanation and targeted analysis, I recommend that the paper proceed to the rebuttal phase for further consideration. | The paper is recommended for acceptance based on its technically sound formulation and practical value in addressing the scarcity of fine-grained annotations for controllable medical image generation. Reviewers recognized the novel application of utilizing a dermatology-specific vision-language model (MONET) to provide continuous image-concept alignment rewards for steering diffusion models via reinforcement learning. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers observed that the method has modest novelty; however, they recommended acceptance based on the effectiveness of the synthetic data generated by the proposed method. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers highlight the contribution of the submission and would like to accept the paper.

title: Volume-Fused Super-Resolution OCT Reveals Cellular-Level Structures in the Outer Segment Across Wider Fields Without Adaptive Optics
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The imaging model in Eq. (1) is notably comprehensive: it jointly accounts for non-uniform motion (via spatiotemporal displacement parameterization), illumination bias (via per-A-scan coefficients with foreground masking), optical distortion (shearing and curvature), and noise. This level of completeness is uncommon in prior OCT super-resolution work and is well motivated by the practical confounders in ophthalmic imaging. 2.The method is purely computational and does not require hardware modifications, pupil dilation, or real-time eye tracking. This represents a significant practical advantage for clinical translation compared to AO-OCT, which demands expensive additional hardware and is restricted to small imaging fields. 3.The reproducibility experiment in Figure 3, where the super-resolution pipeline is applied independently to two disjoint subsets of five volumes each, is a convincing and well-designed validation strategy. It demonstrates that the observed cone reflections are consistent across independent data splits rather than artifacts introduced by the reconstruction. 4.The paper provides a clear and well-structured ablation across intermediate processing stages (single input, fused, supersampled, super-resolved) in Figure 2, which allows the reader to appreciate the incremental contribution of each component. The visual improvements in contrast, sharpness, and separability of cone reflections are substantial. 5.The clinical relevance is clearly articulated: S-cones, which are the likely source of the observed reflections, are known to be more vulnerable in diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa, diabetes, and glaucoma, making them valuable as early biomarkers.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The evaluation is limited to eight healthy volunteers from a single imaging site using a single prototype device. No pathological data are included, which leaves unclear whether the pipeline generalizes to diseased retinas where tissue geometry, reflectivity, and motion patterns may differ substantially. Even a preliminary case or discussion of expected failure modes in pathology would strengthen the paper. 2.The paper lacks quantitative evaluation metrics. All results are presented qualitatively through visual inspection of en face images and B-scans. No resolution measurements (e. g. , Fourier ring correlation, point source analysis), no quantitative comparison against AO-OCT references, and no SNR or contrast-to-noise ratio analysis are reported. This makes it difficult to objectively assess the magnitude of the improvement or compare with other methods. 3.The choice of key hyperparameters, including the upsampling factor (3x), deconvolution sigma_tv = 2.9 um, regularizer weights lambda = 0.2 and gamma = 0.1, and step size delta = 0.12, appears to be fixed without justification or sensitivity analysis. The paper does not discuss how performance varies with these settings or how they should be adapted for different devices, wavelengths, or imaging fields.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper presents a comprehensive approach to the reconstruction of super-resolution images in OCT. The strength of this work lies in the fact that motion artifacts, aberration correction, and resolution enhancement are all addressed within unified mathematical procedures. The authors attempt to provide a comprehensive mathematical description of these procedures. I consider this part to be important, albeit highly abstract.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Major: The authors claim: “This work describes a computational method for reconstructing higher resolution 3D images from repeated (non-AO) retinal OCT volumes by inverting a uniquely comprehensive imaging model.” and describe some sophisticated math in Section 2.However, there is a lack of clarity on how this actually works. My experience with numerical aberration correction using numerical wavefront reforming (e.g., with Zernike polynomial expansion) without adaptive optics demonstrates that achieving super-resolution requires numerical aberration correction with digital beam refocusing to a spot tighter than the initial probing beam. I know this is possible if one locks onto reference points on the retina, corrects the distortions for them to make them sharp structures, and then refocuses more narrowly than the initial beam width. However, the algorithm proposed by the authors is described in highly dense mathematical language, without revealing the physical principles behind such correction and refocusing processes. I would like to see a more detailed explanation in the paper connecting the math to the physical processes, clarifying how and through which operations on physical fields and wavefronts it is possible to compensate, correct, and refocus the beams to achieve super-resolution. I have some doubts regarding reproducibility: there is no mention in the paper whether the data and code are either already hosted somewhere or will be released upon publication so that the community can verify their functionality as described. Most of the operations remain described too abstractly for me, and it is not obvious how they are actually implemented in the algorithms. Personally, I would prefer to recommend such a complex paper for publication only if the code implementation of this algorithm, along with the provided test data, is made openly available for verification, as I do not have full confidence in the reproducibility of these results. Minor: In the mathematical representations, for example in formula (3), the operations should clearly have the meaning of spatial spectrum filtering, represented explicitly as a convolution, or in the Fourier domain as operations on the spectrum. One way or another, distortions and aberrations that occur in OCT arise in k-space, and are usually corrected in this domain, either explicitly (Fourier domain) or in the spatial representation via convolutional functions. This physical meaning should be explicitly stated and described to improve the understanding of the presented algorithm. I would extract the initial parameters of the OCT system and describe them in a separate Methods section. The Methods section currently starts immediately with the algorithm, although it would be great to indicate at the beginning what exactly this is being applied to. Perhaps it would be useful to clearly add this in your response in the rebuttal thread. The following comment is also related to the description of the device and the process: the scanning pattern should be described and illustrated more clearly. It is currently not very clear how the information was acquired and accumulated. The point cloud panel in Fig. 1 does not look informative to me. The citations are not in the correct numerical order based on their appearance in the text (e.g., they jump from 9 to 6, then 25, etc.). Please renumber them sequentially.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This paper achieves cellular-level OCT enhancement without adaptive optics, which improves clinical feasibility. The proposed pipeline is technically comprehensive and addresses multiple acquisition confounders in a unified framework. The qualitative results are also convincing, with clear improvements in sharpness and reproducibility shown in Figures 2 and 3.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited methodological novelty. Several major components in this paper are built directly on the prior work, especially motion correction, illumination compensation, and distortion modeling. 2.The super-resolution stage mainly relies on a classical weighted least-squares formulation related to prior multi-frame super-resolution methods. 3.Evaluation is mostly qualitative and limited to eight healthy-subject datasets.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their careful feedback and positive comments, including “significant practical advantage for clinical translation”, “visual improvements in contrast, sharpness, and separability of cone reflections are substantial”, “a convincing and well-designed evaluation” (Fig. 3, qualitative), “clear and well-structured ablation”, “The clinical relevance is clearly articulated”, “cone reflections are consistent across independent data splits”, “well motivated by the practical confounders”. (Quotes from Reviewer #1.) Subsequently, we focus on major critique, and Reviewer #1, because he provided the worst rating (weak reject). Qualitative Evaluation [Meta,R1,R3] We agree that an extended journal article should include quantitative evaluation. Here, due to the page limit, we prioritized the in our view most tangible and convincing evaluation Our qualitative evaluation (Fig. 3) provides an immediate and intuitive impression of the improvement, and demonstrates its consistency in independent data splits. Multiple instances of each individual improvement (gaps/doubling, cone undistortion, contrast/separability of cone reflections) can be pointed out in a single, small crop. Quantitative evaluation would mix these effects into a single abstract number. It is often chosen to prove subtle/non-obvious improvements, and to compare to prior methods. However, our improvement is visually “substantial”, and since this is a fundamentally novel approach, no directly comparable method exists. The mentioned AO-OCT ground truth only exists in a handful places on earth; we do not have access to paired data. An unpaired comparison image is referenced on p. 7 [16, Fig. 5]. Hyperparameter selection [Meta,R1] 2D-upsampling-factor (3^2=9) should scale with volume repeats (10); sigma_tv was chosen as transverse resolution (9um) / 1D-upsampling-factor 3; regularizer weight controls denoising/blur and should be small; anisotropy factor gamma: small to not blur layers; step size: safe margin below divergence. Added. Limitation to 8 datasets [R1,R3] Core processing steps (motion, illumination, distortion compensation) have been applied to >1000 clinical high-resolution 850nm SD-OCT datasets across diverse pathologies, incl Parkinson’s disease (severe motion) and elderly patients (severe opacities/vignetting). Failure modes are opacities (low illumination) or strong mirror artifacts, if a large portion of the dataset is affected. However, such data is not usable for clinical quantification; compensation is meaningless. Only a handful of the >1000 cases failed due to motion. Added. For our application (OS cones), we wanted to maximize resolution of the initial data, motivating our transition to vis-OCT despite limited data. We expect similar processing behavior in vis-OCT with somewhat increased illumination issues due to a higher sensitivity to opacity of shorter wavelength light. Reproducibility [R3,Meta] Our contribution is an extensive framework that unifies several prior works (motion, illumination & distortion compensation) and adds super-resolution processing. We carefully summarized key ideas of all prior work, but comprehensive reiteration is infeasible in an 8p paper (@R2: there is no appendix anymore); we have to refer to prior papers for implementation details. Reproducibility concern on aberration correction (ACor) [R2] Digital ACor methods use large beam diameters to increase SNR & allow very fast scanning. This scales up aberration effects substantially, but temporal closeness makes them locally consistent, allowing estimation & compensation. Our novel approach: commercial beam diameter & scanning speed, SNR enhancement via averaging, digital super-resolution. Challenges: motion, illumination, distortion. We don’t describe ACor because it is less needed & we are not doing it. Our key message: We achieve substantial improvement without it. Finally, we revised the manuscript for clarity regarding all related comments
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors are expected to provide reasonable explanations for the quantitative analysis and hyperparameter selection to address the reviewers’ concerns. In addition, some reviewers raised concerns regarding the reproducibility of the proposed method. | After reading the rebuttal and other reviewers’ comments, I think the authors have provided reasonable clarifications to the reviewers’ concerns. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a computational 3D super-resolution OCT reconstruction framework for repeated non-adaptive-optics retinal OCT volumes, aiming to reveal cellular-level outer-segment structures over wider fields without adaptive optics hardware or pupil dilation. The reviewers recognized the practical and clinical significance of the work, especially its unified model-based treatment of motion correction, distortion compensation, illumination normalization, and inverse reconstruction. They also appreciated the visually compelling improvement in cone-reflection visibility and the reproducibility experiment using independent data splits. The reviewers raised concerns about the limited quantitative evaluation, small healthy-subject cohort, lack of pathological cases, hyperparameter justification, and reproducibility. In the rebuttal, the authors clarified the rationale behind key hyperparameters, discussed prior experience on a larger set of clinical OCT data, and explained that the current work focuses on computational super-resolution rather than digital aberration correction. Reviewers were satisfied overall, and all post-rebuttal recommendations support acceptance. Although quantitative metrics and broader pathological validation would strengthen an extended version, the paper presents a meaningful and practically relevant framework with convincing qualitative evidence. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a computational framework for reconstructing super-resolved 3D retinal OCT volumes from repeated non-AO scans, aiming to reveal cellular-level outer segment structures over wider fields without adaptive optics. Reviewers agreed that the problem is important and that the practical clinical motivation is strong, especially given the potential to broaden access to microstructural retinal imaging without additional hardware. The unified treatment of motion correction, distortion compensation, illumination normalization, and inverse-model-based reconstruction was also viewed positively. Before rebuttal, the main concerns were the lack of quantitative evaluation, limited validation on only eight healthy subjects from a single site, and insufficient clarity on some methodological and physical aspects of the reconstruction process. The rebuttal addressed these points partially but meaningfully. In particular, the authors clarified the intended scope of the work, explained why paired AO-OCT ground truth and direct quantitative comparisons are not realistically available, provided additional justification for hyperparameter choices, and clarified that core preprocessing steps have already been applied more broadly in their larger clinical experience, even though the present study focuses on a limited vis-OCT dataset for the outer-segment cone application. They also clarified that the method does not rely on digital aberration correction, which helps sharpen the framing of the contribution. The paper still has limitations. Quantitative evaluation remains limited, pathology cases are not included in the current study, and reproducibility would be stronger with public code or more implementation detail. Some of the claims would also benefit from a clearer distinction between what is already validated in the manuscript and what is supported mainly by broader prior experience.

title: When Tissue Speaks: Vibroacoustic Monitoring of Tissue Response During Electrosurgery
reviewer_1_strengths: Clinical relevance: Proposing and analyzing a method for tissue response monitoring, the paper addresses a real and important limitation of conventional electrosurgery which is especially relevant in laparoscopic and robotic settings where perception is limited. This is a clinically well motivated sensing problem that can matter in CAI. Hardware setup and workflow: The hardware setup and sensing workflow provides an elegant solution how to integrate tissue response measurements into electrosurgical applications without disturbing the conventional surgical workflow. Mounting the vibroacoustic sensor proximally on standard instruments allows direct tissue response sensing without requiring custom tool tips or increasing the invasiveness of the intervention.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Phase transition claim: From the experiments performed for scenario I, the claim that the observed phase-dependent changes appear consistent with thermally induced tissue transformations is hard to verify from the performed experiments as no real indicators (e. g. tissue temperature) of the transition from one tissue transformation phase into the other is provided. This leaves this part of the paper in the speculative, a more thorough investigation including real-world reference measures would be required. Tissue differentiation claim: While the performed analysis provide some indication that tissue differentiation can be possible with this method, a proper analysis should include a hold out test set to establish differentiation performance Methodological reproducibility: The methodological description lacks detail to allow for straightforward reproduction of the method. In particular, the description of the implementation and parametrization of the individual processing steps remains rather vague. Statistical rigor: The authors claim statistical significance for their results shown in Fig. 3e but do not provide statistical tests, confidence intervals or similar to support this claim.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: S1 : Electrosurgical tissue state monitoring is an open clinical problem. The VA sensing solution is not invasive, tool agnostic and addresses a gap not covered by existing systems (impedance or acoustic based methods) S2 : Scenario 1 (temporal evolution) and Scenario 2 (tissue type differentiation) address two clinically relevant and separate questions, providing a more complete picture. S3 : Signal analyisis choice: four indicators (homomorphic envelope, peak density, stationary CWT, normalized stationary CWT) capture complementary elements of the signal. S4 : No instrument modification is a strong practical contribution. S5 : Data and code will be released on acceptance, bolstering reproducibility. S6 : Experiment performed by an experienced surgeon with a standardized protocol.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: W1 : Boxplots for phase wise band energy contributions (Fig. 3e, 3f) reported but have no p-values, confidence intervals, nor statistical tests. Paired Wilcoxon tests or similar would be expected with N=15 in Scenario 1.The lack of quantitative significance data is a big methodological gap. W2 : Phase transitions (~2.3 s, ~7.5 s) are identified from a representative single trial, then used to segment all 15 trials, then boxplots are computed. The method does not verify if transitions occur at consistent times across trials or if data driven phase detection phase detection would yield the same structure. W3 : All tissue is ex vivo porcine. In vivo involves perfusion, blood oozing, varying tissue hydration etc… Extension to in vivo scenarios is entirely unexplored. W4 : N=15 for S1 and N=10 per tissue for S2 : with small sample sizes, overfitting becomes an issue when using UMAP (https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03426, Section 6)
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper is the first to use vibrations (called “vibroacoustics”) to learn more about tissue during electrosurgery. It’s a new way to get information, going beyond just looking and measuring electricity. The sensor is designed to easily attach to existing surgical tools without needing any changes to how surgeons work or putting anything inside the patient’s body The experiments were designed very well to test different aspects of the technique (how vibrations change over time and how they differ between tissues). They followed a clear plan and were done consistently.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: -The authors should clarify whether the UMAP + kNN analysis is intended as descriptive visualization or as a predictive classifier. If the former, the classifier framing and claims of ‘complete separability’ and ‘robust differentiation’ should be softened. If the latter, a proper cross-validation (e.g., leave-one-out given n=30) should be reported with accuracy metrics.” Another potential limitation is the extremely small sample size (only 30 total samples across all tissue types). reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for the constructive feedback. All reviewers recognized the clinical relevance, novelty, and translational potential of the proposed vibroacoustic (VA) sensing approach for electrosurgery. Regarding the concern about statistical support for the reported phase differences, Scenario I aims to show that VA signals evolve systematically during electrosurgical coagulation, revealing reproducible signal changes up to tissue carbonization. Fig. 3(a–d) illustrates the temporal evolution of the VA signal, while Fig. 3(e,f) was intended to generalize these observations across the 15 independently analyzed VA data from a signal perspective, rather than to provide statistical validation of tissue-state transitions. Across VA signals, consistent redistribution of energy between LF/MF/HF bands and reduced total spectral energy in the late phase were observed. We apologize if some wording suggested stronger statistical claims. The interpretation of these behaviors as thermally induced tissue transformations was intended as hypothesis-driven, consistent with established thermal tissue literature and the manuscript conclusion that the biological interpretation is based on indirect evidence and requires validation. Regarding the clarification on how phase transitions were determined and their consistency across trials, we apologize if the methodological description was not sufficiently clear. In the manuscript, signals were described as segmented according to transition points identified during the qualitative analysis. However, the manual annotation procedure was not described explicitly enough. The transition points shown in the representative example were not transferred to all signals. Instead, phase transitions were independently identified for each VA signal through manual annotation based on changes observed in the CWT spectrum and band-energy indicators. The goal was to characterize systematic changes in VA signal behavior during coagulation. The temporal duration of the phases naturally varied across signals. The reproducible aspect was therefore not fixed transition timing, but the consistent evolution of VA signal behavior during coagulation. Regarding the descriptive or predictive role of the UMAP/kNN analysis, Scenario II was intended as a descriptive exploratory analysis rather than a predictive classification framework. UMAP was used as an unsupervised visualization of the extracted VA indicators without tissue labels, while the kNN boundaries were included only to illustrate local label consistency. Therefore, the observed grouping reflects structure inherently present in the extracted signal features rather than supervised optimization toward tissue classes. Regarding tempering claims about tissue differentiation given the small dataset, we agree that the current ex vivo dataset is limited and does not support strong claims regarding generalizability. Scenario II should therefore be interpreted as exploratory evidence that different tissues exhibit distinguishable VA behaviors in this controlled setting. Regarding reproducibility, the methodology combines standard signal-processing methods with the proposed VA sensing framework. Therefore, the manuscript focused primarily on the sensing concept and signal behaviors rather than low-level implementation details. For clarification, the pseudo-frequency bands were identified from recurrent spectral activity patterns consistently observed across signals, and all processing steps were applied using fixed parameters. The planned release of code and data will allow full reproducibility and inspection of the processing pipeline. Overall, we believe the work fits well within the MICCAI scope and evaluation criteria. The paper addresses a clinically relevant CAI problem, introduces a novel sensing concept with translational potential, and presents systematic exploratory experiments supporting the feasibility of the proposed approach.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Given the mixed but generally borderline-positive reviews, I recommend inviting a rebuttal. Several key concerns: (1) provide stronger statistical support for the reported phase differences; (2) clarify how phase transitions were determined and whether they are consistent across trials; (3) clarify whether UMAP/kNN is descriptive or predictive, and provide proper cross-validation if predictive claims are made; (4) temper claims about tissue differentiation given the small ex vivo sample size; and (5) improve methodological detail for reproducibility. | Reviewers recognized the novelty, clinical relevance, and translational appeal of the proposed sensing concept. Following the rebuttal, two reviewers were satisfied with the clarification that the UMAP/kNN analysis is descriptive rather than predictive, and that phase transitions were annotated independently per trial rather than transferred from a single representative example. However, one reviewer still has concerns regarding the validation and lack of objective reference measurements of tissue state, such as temperature or tissue-damage indicators. Overall, the rebuttal appropriately tempered some claims and clarified the exploratory nature of the work, but concerns remain regarding statistical rigor and biological validation. Given the novelty and potential impact of the sensing approach, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The rebuttal has not addressed the validation questions raised by the first reviewer, which are important in understanding the value of the proposed work. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers’ concerns have been successfully addressed in the rebuttal, making the work a solid contribution especially for what concerns clinical applications in CAI.

title: Where Is the Needle Tip? VA Sensing Reveals Hidden Needle-Tissue Transitions During US Guidance
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of US-guided needle guidance, which is a known challenge. By adding VA, the authors demonstrate for the first time that tissue-to-tissue needle transitions could be detected even in cases where the needle was poorly visualized under US imaging. The authors use reasonably realistic phantoms and perform 42 seperate insertions, giving great confidence in the presented data being reproducible. The signal processing steps are reasonably well described.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Some key parameters are missing, making it impossible for readers to reproduce the work: specifications of the VA sensor are absent: what is its bandwidth, sampling rate, and in which direction(s) does it sense? How many DoFs, if more than one? Neither the figures nor the video show scale bars, so as reader I am left guessing at the scale of the tissue layers, imaging depths, needle insertion velocities etc. Figs. 3+4 do not have units (fig 4) or any labels (fig 3). 42 needle insertions were performed, but it is not stated whether these were performed at different positions, phantoms, velocities, insertion angles, etc. How diverse were these repeat measurements? What was (approximately) the insertion velocity? In addition, the signal processing could have been described r motivated in greater detail: Why was Wasserstein distance chosen as key metric, what is special about it? Would there have been alternatives or superior options? “an interactionsensitive frequency band is extracted” is insufficiently clear - the authors do not specify the values of this band here, and only mention it on page 6 “in passing”. Similar choices (e. g. the window length of the moving window, and the exact choice of reference window(s)) should also be clarified. Finally, the paper is in my opinion too light on the clinical implications: a ca. 1s difference between US and VA transition times (Fig. 5) is significant and would arguably make any kind of guidance meaningless. What was the needle insertion speed, i. e. , what were the depth uncertainties corresponding to these timing differences? What precision is required? Arguably, the centimetre-regime (I assume; no scale bars provided) demonstrated here is of limited value, as that level of accuracy is certainly attainable using US imaging - or even markings on the needle. Image guidance becomes crucial at the (sub) millimetre scales; how would the method perform here? The video is a useful addition, but mostly casts “doubt” on the accuracy of the extraction of t_tc. I appreciate your algorithms specify this is the true time, but looking at the Wasserstein distance, arguably the regime change occurs BEFORE the software-determined t_tc in all three (high/mid/low visibility) cases. Especially when mm-scale scenarios are targeted, this could cause significant issues. The text does not specify, but the video suggests all needle insertions were performed at constant velocity, which is not representative of actual needle placement, where image guidance informs repositioning and motion is often non-uniform. How will the VA method hold up in these cases, as vibrations due to “jagged” motion could well mask the VA signals?
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Major strengths: 1.This paper addresses a persistent need in ultrasound imaging to localize needle tips even under variable visibility conditions and presents an approach without the need for burdensome hardware and workflow changes. 2.The evaluation is generally comprehensive within the space constraints of the paper and strongly supports the validity of the proposed approach. 3.The paper is well-written and logical, with attractive, easily interpreted figures.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Major weaknesses: 1.The primary weakness of this paper is the incremental novelty of the work. Although the paper well-done and does not overstate the impact, the contributions represent only small advancements over previous works and there appears to be missing relevant works on similar topics that are not acknowledged. For example, Sühn et al. (Vibro-acoustic sensing of tissue-instrument-interactions allows a differentiation of biological tissue in computerised palpation. title: X-Edit: Exact, Explicit, and Explainable Null-Space Editing for Medical Vision Transformers
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses an important issue: how to correct failure cases in deployed medical ViTs without catastrophic forgetting. This is meaningful for me. The overall method is more principled than simple fine-tuning and more interpretable than purely heuristic editing. On the reported benchmarks, X-Edit achieves strong edit success rates while substantially reducing test accuracy drop relative to FT/EWC/LWE. The anonymous repository is well organized, which further strengthens the paper’s completeness and reproducibility, and makes the work a potentially useful baseline for follow-up research.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The mathematical guarantee is notable narrower than the paper’s framing suggests. The method starts from an anchor-constrained editing objective, but the actual derivation only guarantees invariance of the edited layer’s linear mapping on the finite anchor-induced key subspace, which is, (W+\Delta WP)K_0 = WK_0.However, it is not equivalent to preserving the full model behavior on the true test or deployment distribution. Likewise, the closed-form solution is exact only for the surrogate quadratic objective used in the derivation, not for the original nonlinear model-editing problem or for downstream clinical risk. I therefore believe the claims around “exact,” “safe,” “trustworthy,” and “lifelong clinical deployment” are overstated and should be substantially toned down. A minor concern is that, include other continual learning and editing baselines would be helpful to position the work.

reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically critical problem: correcting model errors without catastrophic forgetting, which is essential for safe deployment of AI in healthcare. The theoretical grounding is strong, with mathematical guarantees provided through null-space projection constraints. The closed-form solution for parameter updates is computationally efficient compared to iterative gradient-based methods, making it practical for real-world deployment. The integration of causal tracing with null-space editing provides an interpretable and controllable intervention mechanism. Comprehensive evaluation across six diverse medical imaging benchmarks demonstrates robust generalization. The proposed DPE (Drop Per Edit) metric effectively quantifies the editing trade-off between correction success and collateral damage. The authors provide anonymized code access, supporting reproducibility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: LIMITED THEORETICAL NOVELTY: The null-space editing approach is adapted from recent work in LLM editing (AlphaEdit, MEND). While the application to medical ViTs is new, the core technical contribution is incremental. INSUFFICIENT ANALYSIS OF EDIT SCOPE: The paper does not thoroughly analyze how the number of edited samples affects performance. Real clinical scenarios may require editing on hundreds of cases, not just the small edit sets reported. LACK OF CROSS-DOMAIN EVALUATION: All experiments are conducted within the same domain as the training data. The framework’s robustness to domain shifts (e.g., different hospitals, scanners) is not evaluated. MISSING ABLATION ON CAUSAL TRACING: The paper does not ablate the causal tracing component to demonstrate its necessity compared to simply editing fixed layers across all samples. LIMITED COMPARISON WITH SOTA: While LWE is included as a baseline, other recent model editing methods for vision models are not compared. NO ANALYSIS OF EDIT ACCUMULATION: The sequential editing capability is claimed but not thoroughly validated with long edit sequences (e.g., 100+ sequential edits).
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A major strength of the paper is that it addresses a highly relevant problem for medical AI: how to fix model errors after deployment without degrading previously learned diagnostic capability. This is an important and practical setting in clinical environments, where naive fine-tuning can be unsafe.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the paper’s novelty seems to come more from adapting and integrating existing ideas than from introducing a fundamentally new editing principle. The use of null-space constrained editing is closely related to prior work such as AlphaEdit and related transformer editing methods, while causal tracing and ViT editing are also already explored in prior literature. Therefore, the paper’s novelty is meaningful at the application/integration level, but the conceptual leap may be somewhat incremental. Another weakness is that the evaluation, while broad across datasets, is still limited in terms of clinical realism and scale. Several experiments involve a very small number of edit samples, such as only 3 edited cases for OrganAMNIST and 8 for LiFS-subtask2, which makes it harder to judge robustness under larger-scale or repeated editing scenarios.

author_feedback: ## Novelty R3 & R4: The conceptual novelty feels incremental compared to LLM editing methods. R: Thanks. We agree that X-Edit is inspired by recent null space editing methods in LLMs. However, the contribution of our work is to reformulate this principle for medical ViTs, where the edited knowledge is visual diagnostic behavior rather than textual factual associations. This requires a different localization mechanism, a different representation preservation constraint, and a clinically motivated evaluation protocol. We will clarify in the camera-ready. ## Methods R3 & R4: Raised concerns about the small number of edit samples in some datasets and requested validation for large-scale, sequential editing. R: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. The relatively small edit sets in some datasets come from our protocol: D_edit consists of naturally misclassified samples from a disjoint validation split, reflecting the intended post-hoc correction setting. Therefore, the edit size is determined by the actual failure cases of the base model. We also note that X-Edit is designed to support sequential editing. In Eq. (4) and Eq. (5), previously edited keys are explicitly included to reduce interference with past edits. Due to the limited space, we focused on the main multi-dataset reliability comparison and did not report extensive large-scale sequential curves. We will clarify this design choice and limitation in the revision. ## Writing R2: The mathematical guarantees apply strictly to the finite anchor-induced subspace and surrogate quadratic objective, recommending toning down absolute claims like exact, safe, and lifelong. R: We thank the reviewer for this important clarification. We agree that the mathematical guarantee of X-Edit should be interpreted within its formal scope, namely the finite anchor-induced null space and the surrogate quadratic objective. Specifically, the projection preserves anchor representations, while the closed-form update provides an exact solution to the defined editing objective. It should not be interpreted as a global guarantee over all unseen samples or clinical deployment scenarios. We will revise the manuscript to make this scope explicit and tone down absolute claims. ## Experiments R3: Requested causal tracing ablations and domain shift evaluations. R: We thank the reviewers for these constructive suggestions. We agree that causal tracing ablations and explicit domain-shift evaluations would further strengthen the empirical analysis. In this work, we focused the limited space on validating the core editing objective across multiple medical imaging benchmarks, emphasizing whether X-Edit can correct targeted errors while preserving test-set performance. Due to the page limit, we did not include exhaustive ablations on the causal tracing module or broader domain-shift protocols. We will clarify this limitation in the revised manuscript and consider these evaluations as important future work. R2 & R3: Suggested comparing against additional editing and continual learning baselines. R: We appreciate the reviewers’ suggestion. In the current submission, we compared X-Edit with representative baselines including fine-tuning, fine-tuning with L2 regularization, EWC, LWE, and retraining, covering standard adaptation, continual-learning-based preservation, ViT editing, and an empirical upper bound. Due to the limited space, we were unable to include a more exhaustive set of editing and continual learning methods. We will acknowledge this limitation more clearly and extend the comparison to broader baselines in future work.
